div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

SCHOOLMASTER : "What is the best conductor of sound?" Small Boy: "Please, sir, a tom-cat on the tiles." THE FORCE or HABIT. —" Now, wifey, begin with your curtain lecture, else I shan't get to asap. EASIEST WAY TO MARK TABLR-LINEN. —Leave a baby and some blsck-curreut jam alone at the table for three minutes. THE OTHEL WAY. —Claribel : "Do you think I would marry Smith if I wanted to spite Jones?" Marie: " Ceutainly not. You'd marry Jones." MRS. ITOUNGWED (anxiously) : "Do you think darling baby's lungs are sound, John?" Mr. Younowed (sadly) "Alas ! yes; they're all sound'!" GREENLAND has no cats. How th3nkful the Greenlanders should be. Imagine cats in a country where the nights are six months long. AN AWKWARD MISTAKE. —Gent : "I must say, Madam, that you carry your age remarkably well; you look almost as young as your daughter !" Lady: "Why, lam the daughter!" A CONTEMPORARY mentions a case beyond the ordinary oculist. It is that of a young lady . who, instead of a pupil, has a college student in her eye. "MIGHT I ask who lives here ?" asked a polite gentleman of a stranger he met in front of a hand- some mansion. "Certainly, sir," as politely res- ponded the other. "Who is it, sir?' "I'm sure I don't know," replied the stranger.

PHILANTHROPIST : "What's the matter, my man?" Dejected Individual : "I am one of those whose employment has been taken from them by . the fashion of woman's dress." "What is your business?" "Street-sweeper." _ .
JORNSON : "When I do marry I intend to marry a sensible g rl, if I can find one." Tomson : "Now, there's Miss Sharpe ; she gave me up.' Johnson : "Just the girl I want. Won't you introduce

?" MAN is awfully clever in some things, but nobody has ever discovered one who could jam a hat-pin clean through his bead and make it come out at the other side, as the women do. "DOCTOR, when do you think a man weighs ine.st?" asked a patient who was undergoing a course of dietary treatment. " When he steps on my corns," answered the doctor. A CHANNEL FOR LITERARY ASPIRANTS. —" I shall find another channel for my article," wrote the author of a rejected contribution. "That's right,' was the answer of the courteous country editor? "the British Channel would be an excel- lent place for it." FIRST LADY (to new-found friend) : "You are the most fortunate of women. I did not believe such a perfect angel of a man could exist. He handed you that money with as little hesitation as if he had been a lover, instead of the husband of years." Second Lady (quietly) : It's my money." JUST BY WAY OF A CHANGE.—Policeman (at sight, three sheets in the wind) : " mister, can you tell me—hic--whish is my beat?" AN EMPTY Vono.—Physician : "Considering the weak state of your eyes, it will be as well if you gaze as much as possible into empty space." Patient: "All right, then, keep looking into my purse !" Mils HOMESPUN, who has a terrible time every morning to get her young brood out of their beds, says she cannot understand why children are called the rising generation. A FARSfER invented a scarecrow recently which seems to have worked with wonderful effect. It not oely scared off every crow that saw it, but one ' .crow was so frightened by the invention that he brought back the corn which he had stolen three .days before. BLINICERS "One never loses anything by keep- ing his engagements punctually." Winkers : "My -.experience is he is apt to lose half an hour's time waiting for the other fellow." JACK Hannur (with unwonted enthusiasm): "By Jove! I see that some fellow is talking about introducing a bill into the House, making it a mis- ,demeanour to send annoying letters to anyone. Very clever idea that. I'll have my tailor locked ap for six months, by Jove!" SCHOOLMASTER: "Scientists tell us the moon is inhabited." George (from the bottom of the class) : "Then where do the people go when there is only a half moon?" LONDON MILIDIAN : "Good gracious what's that? Mary, bring my gun quick—a wild beast is in the yard." Mary (who was once in the country) "Why, sir, that a cow." " Lor, you don't say .so ! " CLARA : "Harry proposed to me last night, and I accepted him." Helen (triumphantly) : "Why, he proposed to me last week, and I refused him." Clara (coolly): "Yes, I know it. He told me he did it just for practice. He knew You didn't care for him." "How long," says a contemporary, "can one live without air? ' It depends on the air. Most people could live a long time without some of the airs which have been popular during the last twelvemonth. A Maar from the provinces, who was paying a long visit to London, found his hair was leaving him at the top of his head, and took his barber to task about it. "You sold me two bottles of stuff to make the hair grow." "It is very strange it won't grow again," said the artist in hair; "I •can't understand it." " Look here," said the .countryman, "I don't mind drinking another bottle, but this must be the last." THAT ALTERS THE CASE. —" Sir, there are several beggars at the door." "Kick them out!" "But, sir, they are some of your electors." "Ah ! the dear fellows; show them in ! "

- "Mr dear," said her husband, gently rousing his wife —the lady was dangerously in—" Mrs. , Hobson called a little while ago and left her love I and sympathy for you. She seems deeply affected." -"John,' said the sick lady, in a very weak tone of voice, as she slowly unclosed her eyes, "what did ahe have on?" "Mv dear young lady," said a gushing artist to her, "you are positively lovely ! Wouldn't you like me to do you in oils?" "Sir," exclaimed her father's wide, indignantly, "do you take me for a aardine ENFA:irr TERRIBLE.—HOSt (to visitor) ; l what a pity you did not come a minute sooner; my wife has only just cleared away the coffee Little Moritz: "Yes, and she nearly broke a cup in her hurry '' WAGAWAY: "So you heard my lectures on 'Miracles.' Do you know what a miracle is, my little girl?" Bessie : "Oh, yes. My sister said it would be a Miracle if you didn't stay for dinner to-day." As William bent over her fair face he whis- pered, : "Darling, if I should ask you in French if I might kiss you, what would you answer?" She, summoning hr scanty knowledge of French, replied : don't ! "I usno to find time hanging on my hands, but I etei t now. The days seem to fly." "Then you are happY ?" "No, ['in not. " Well, air, after the ceremony she will be my wife." SOLD AGAIN —A : "What is Meyer doing , -now !" B: ".L saw him a little while ago with .his head in a noose, a knife at his throat, and foaming at the month." A : " Horrible I Where? Where?" CDIIIO and warm yourself in mine. All you've got to do is to get a Irian to bring your coke here. In that way you will save the expense of a stove." GrnITLEMAN (savagely, to hairdresser): "You ti in l That stuff you warranted to do away with the bald patches I had has taken every hair off my -head." Hairdresser : " Well, it has done away -with the bald patches, sir. Your head's bald all ova" now.".

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

The Unionist Whips are trying hard to keep the Government majorities down, and by desperate expedients which earlier in the cession were not heard of. They are refusing pairs except to Minis- terialists who can come and vote if required, and are keeping every available man at the House. They went :he length on Tuesday of refusing to pair with Mr. W. A. M'Arthur, one of the Govenment Whips, who was kept at home by illness. In order, there- fore, to use his vote, Mr. M'Arthur had come down to the House at great risk, and sat wrapped up near the fire in the Liberal Whips' room. Having got down to the 'House, the Unionist Whips paired him, and spared him the necessity of walking through the lobbies, but they intimated that they would not continue the pair if be was kept at home.

One of the few remaining links of the Wesley family has passed away through the death of Miss Eliza Wesley, a granddaughter of Charles Wesley of hymn-book fame. All her life Miss Wesley had been associated with the Church of England, and for the past forty years was organist in one of the London churches. Richly endowed with the musical genius of the Wesley family, her talents were developed by her famous father, Samuel Wesley. One of her brothers died organist of Gloucester Cathedral; another, Mr. R. Glen Wesley, is now organist at John Wesley's Chapel, City-road. I learn that Miss Wesley, who lived at Islington, has left many letters of interest which were addressed to her father by Weber, Mendelssohu, Rossini, and other celebrities.

The Jews in the Hampstead district of London I are at present plunged in the very interesting and exciting'controversy whether or not an organ shall be introduced into the Hampstead Synagogue. Voting papers have been tent round •by the board of management to the Jews resident in Hampstead, asking them to vote on this burning question. It is well known that the Chief Rabbi in London is op- posed to any such innovation, as he expreQsed, some years ago,a strong opinion against it. But it seems to be open to the managers of synap,agues to do as they please in the matter, and if the Hamp- stead Synagogue leads the way and sots an example it may give a great stimulus to a movement which is creating much interest in the Jewish world. The Jews resident in Melbourne' on the other ride of the globe, have already gone through the throes of a similar controversy, and settled it in favour of the organ; but not without years of discussion. They have even gone a step further, and introduced a mixed choir of male andfemale voices. Why there should be any objection either to the organ or the mixed choir is not clear to an Englishman, looking to the great part played by music in services of the Temple in early times.

There is not much probability that the renewal of the controversy as to the titles by which our re- giments are to be distinguished will lead to a re versal of the present nomenclature, cumbersome and somewhat stupid though it be. The old system of distinguishing a regiment by a mere number had at least the merit of simplicity; but so might territorial or geographical aesignation, if simpli- city hid been kept in view in selecting the titles. The name of a regiment has now Come to be loaded with words to a degree that rivals those of Royal personages, and probably there are many soldiers in every battalion who do not know its correct name. The recognition of local sentiment or patriotism sha much to recommend it, and so has the adoption of a race or clan name, and in the case of many Highland regiments. These, it is true, are not alto- gether discarded; but it is well-known that a York- shire regiment is no more made up of Yorkshiremen than a Highland regiment is of Highlanders. The Horse guards are considering the possibility or desirability of creating greater simplicity, but it will surely scarcely be by going back to the old numbers.-

-- A correspondent of a London paper writes :—" I see that the inscription on the bronze coinage is in future to bear the letters Ind. Imp.' in addition to the words Britt Regina.' How does this square with Mr. Disraeli's assurance to the Rouse of Commons, made during the passing of the Royal Styles and Titles Bill, that her Majesty's new title should never be used in England ?"

Lord Rosebery looks better after his little sea- trip, although in appearance he has somewhat aged. His hair, which was only slightly tinted with grey. a year ago,is greyer to-day. Dr. Broadbent saw him on Monday afternoon, and his report was that, cen- sidering the rough weather which the yachting party had experienced in the Channel, there had been considerable improvement. There was no truth whatever in the report which was widely current in the lobby of the House of Commons at the beginning of the week of Lord Rosebery's reAignation, The delay in the Queen's departure, which gave rise to the report, was due entirely to her desire to remain in town for the reception of the Ameer's son.

There is still plenty of enthusiasm and energy left in the Liberal party is shown by the fact that, in response to an urgent whip, Mr. J. Williamson positively chartered a'special train from Lancaster to London on Tuesday in order to enable him to be in the House in good time for the early Committee divisions on the Welsh Church Bill. '

There is indignation as well as amusement felt at the attempts made in certain Tory quarters to hit Lord Rosebery unfairly. The comments referred to are in exceptionally had taste. The motive is transparent, and the spirit is malignant to a degree happily unusual in political con- troversy. Possibly with a view to influencing pending elections and of damaging the collective And united action of Liberals in the House, the absurd statement is made that Lord Rosebery is on the point of resigning, that his health thoroughly incapacitates him from discharging his great duties, and that even his appearances in the lobby and at the County Council are meant to conceal the I truth and keep up appearances a little longer. This is all malicious nonsense Lord Rosebery has not yet shaken off entirely tl)e effects of his illness, but he is rapidly regaining his usual strength. The i best information s that he has not entertained and is not entertaining in the most remote degree the intention of withdrawing from public life •, and that, on the contrary, he is about to take, as before his illness, the decisive part in shaping the policy of the party during the rest of the session.

The Parliamentary golfers are bringing their tournament very near its close. There are now only eigt.t players left in it. All the representa- tives of Lancashire have disappeared from the field. Mr. T. W. Legh and Mr. Seton-Karr st)od well into I the fourth round, and the former ought certainly to have got into the fifth, but they went down be- fore two press gallery men, either of whom has now a very fair chance of winning the match. The favourite, however, is Mr. Herbert Gladstone. He has gone very keenly into the tournament ; he ham kept himself in good practice at Littlestone and elsewhere ; and he has so far played rather better I than his handicap.

--- Wednesday was set apart by society for coaching. In Most brilliant weather the road coaches met at 11.30 on the Horse Guards' Parade, and with a fair number of passengers went on their several routes —some to Richmond and Windsor, others to Esher and Sandown, while one went as far as Southend. 'The pick of the turnout was as usual the" Old Times" coach, tooled by Mr. Harveyson, and the next best was the "New Times," driven by Mr. Shoolbred, who led the teams. At one o'clock society turned , out in great wirnbers to wirnsss the first meet of the Four-in-Hand Club at the Magazine. Hyde Park when the extravagance of the ladies' new dresses I divided attention with the teams. Lord Allingten again carried off the ralm with his black browns, and Baron Dutchman came in a good sec...md. The new members, especially the Duke of Marlborough, had good teams, and their coaches were full. The plainest turnout, yet the most wmkmanlike, was Lord Londonderry's, This consisted of three dark bays and an off leader of pure white. No member of Royalty graced the show.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 25. 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 25. 1895.
LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NI/E, At last we are having some really sunny days, and we must get our summer costumes ready. This black satin mantle is intended for bright sunny days when the north and east winds have gone to sleep. The peculiarity is the cape on each shoulder, tied in at the waist and finished with a sash bow and long ends. The ruffle is of black satin ribbon, and spring flowers are pinned or stitched into it at pleasure. This style of mantle is most welcome to ladies who have slight, pretty Egures, as it really shows them off so much better than those that conceal the arms and ignore the 'roundness of the natural form.

Blouses are as pretty as ever. A charming one is of pink cambric, the yoke gathered, and slashed with rows of Swiss insertion, and the lower part simply gathered on and drawn in at the waist with a crossed belt. The sleeves are quite new, having a starched gauntlet, edged with insertion at the elbow, and continued thence close-fitting to the wrist. Now that the sming eleN.ning is over we may begin putting up such things as mantel borders. At many shops are to be had designs cut out of stout paper, which are inten.lcil to be used for the• fashionable appliqué trimmings for capes and dresses. By procuring one of these, cutting it out in velvet and pasting it down on the cloth or serge, and running the sewing machine round the margin of the velvet, thus securing it to the foundation, we have the beginning of a very effective style of decoration. The raw edges May be worked over with fine gold cord, or with buttonhole stitches of coloured silk, or with a wire braid, or anything else of the sort that may suggest itself. - . Diagnosis of Love. I came across the following diagnosis of love the other day, which since it is such a universal subject of in- terest, will, doubtless, be welcomed : Love—A nervous disorder affecting the entire system and sometimes even the clothes and food of the victim. Peculiar to both sexes of all ages, from childhood to second childhood. Always fatal in age, seldom in youth. Symptoms : Loss of appetite and interest in mun- dane affairs. Anxiety as to persbnal appearance. Long- ing for flowers and poetry. Demented belief in the ab- solute perfection of some being of the opposite sex. Vacant expression of the eyes and cerebral cavity. 'Patient speaks in monosyllables, and takes an especial interest in the monosyllable " Yes." Treatment : One dose of the monosyllable "No," and nursing for males. For fsmales a new sealskin sacque, diamonds, and a trip to Paris are sometimes efficacieus. An application of " stern parents" may be of use,but more often merely excites the malady. Marriage is an absolute specific. But it is so dan- gerous that it is never used except in extreme cases.

Spring-Cleaning. Spring-cleaning time always seems to be a time for the trial of tempers and digestions. It tries men's souls,and is even harder for women to bear. House-cleaning time, however, can be made endurable even to the masculine mind by strict adherence to one simple rule. Clean one room at a time. Do not have the entire house upset and odoroug of soap suds and furniture polish. Let every- thing be done decently and in order, and " all will be well," as the old-fashioned heroine used to remark. Bread crumbs are amongst the house-cleaner's best friends. Crushed to a coarse powder, they may be used 'to clean delicate lamp-shades, screens, and decorative trifles dear to the heart '1 hey will also remove grease spots from wall-papers, and are invaluable in freshening wall-papers that have become dingy. Dough is also excellent for cleaning wall-papers. Every good house- wife should superintend and take part in spring-cleaning if she wishes it to be thoroughly done. Those who are afraid of spoiling their hands can wear loose rubber gloves. She should keep a special uniform for house- cleaning time, which can be readily washed.

Pure Drinking Water. The problem of supplying pure drinking water in thickly settled districts is becoming a very grave one, and it is worth while to give it the most serious co n- sideration. It is a fact well known by sanitary experts, that after long periods of dry weather, succeeded by very heavy rains, the death-rate increases with surprising rapidity. Fevers and other germ diseases, multiply until an epid- emic is threatened. The great mistake people make on the water question is in supposing that water that looks, tastes and smells' Perfectly clean is necessarily all right. When we take into consideration that the germs of the most deadly dis- eases are discoverable only with the aid of the most powerful microscope, we may readily understand how a few millions of them, more or less, may be taken into the system without our knowledge. Once settled intheir comfortable environment, they grow and nourish until the mischief is too far advanced to be counteracted. Every family should have a good filter, and that filter should be renewed as often as once in two or four weeks, according to the condition of the water. Very few people realise what a deadly thing an impure filter is. Instead of removing the cause, it simply amounts to a carefully-swept and garnished residence for ' myriads of disease germs of various kinds. The sand and charcoal filter is very good as tar as it goes, but :needs constant renewing. And this is, to many people, so much trouble that they complacently swallow bacteria and baccilli by the hundred thous- ands. It is not a good plan under any circumstances to put ice into water. Ice, especially that gathered in thickly populated districts, is said to be the essence of all im- purity, and it is not at all unlikely that the distress and illness attributed to ice water is caused not so much by the!cold as by the presence of countless germs that attack the system. It is important that every person drink at least several pints of water a day. and it is easy to imagine, if the water is impure, the amount of poison that one may take within twenty-four hours. Water probably rv- ceives as little attention as anything about the house. Pure water is one of the first necessities for health, and one which no householder should for a moment think of holding as a secondary consideration.

CHAPTER XXIX. SAVED Br LOVE. IN an instant the greatest excitement prevailed. \Vas the young man mad, to risk his life so reek- ics ly among the wild, dashing breakers? they asked themselves, breathlessly. They strained their eyes and held their breath. It certainly looked as though two lives would be lost instead of one. Prayers went up from women's hearts ; men muttered, hoarsely, "God strengthen his arm l" and through the moments that followed they watched with bated breath, the intense silence brosen only by the loud, hoarse murmurs of the breakers. Frederick Thornton was young and strong, and au expert swimmer, but the odds were fearfully against him. He struck out bravely for the shin- ing mark that was drifting out so swiftly to sea. The waves, hissing, boiling and churning around him, seemed to laugh in wild glee at his efforts to cheat them of their prey. Down, down he struck after her, swifter than arrow-flight, drenched, choked, blimlod by wave and spray, and an instant later he turned and struck boldly for the shore, holding the form of Doris in his arms. But reaching the shore was no easy task. The great waves beat him back, and his utmost efforts seemed to prove futile, as, sure as fate, he realised they were drifting out to

sea. He saw the life-boat that was put out, but could it reach them? Could his strength last that long? He was strong and sinewy, yet it was no light task to hold that heavy burden with his left arm, striking out with the right. All this occurred to the girl who clung to him. "Leave me, Frederick,' she gasped, piteously. 'lt will be all you can do to save yourself." "I'll never leave you while I have life You would be swept down in a minute. We will live or die together !" he cried, holding her fast, and bat thug heroically with the waves. "Go I—leave me to myfate !" she panted, wildly. "Go—for my sake, Frederick—because I—love—
you!' And with those words she fell back in his arms in
a dead faint. Perhaps it was those words that imbued him with new life, and buoyed him up until the life-boat . _ _ .
reached him. A few minutes later, amidst lusty cheers and glad cries, Frederick Thornton laid Doris down on the sand among the throng that had assembled
there. From that hour handsome Frederick Thornton WilA the hero and idol of the belles of Newport. It was a week before Doris was sufficiently recovered to venture down to the parlour to thank

him for saving her life. It was evening; the chandeliers were lighted, throwing a soft, mellow light over the halls and vast parlours, and out upon the stretch of beach beyond lying so white in the clear, bright star.

„ light. Doris saw him out on the veranda, pacing to and fro, smoking a cigar. Silently she crossed the ver- anda and stood before him, like a vision in her cling ng dress of soft fleecy white. "1 am come to thank you for what you have done for me, Mr. Thornton,” she said, with an unconscious flutter in her voice, extending both her hands. "I thank you so much words will not express my indebtedness. Why did you do it? It might have cost you your own life. Oh !why did you do so much for me, Mr. Thorn- __

ton ?" He took both her trembling hands. "We will walk down on the beach together, and I will tell you why," he answered. How smooth the treacherous, smiling sea looked under the brilliant starlight. How clear the silver moon looked, coyly hiding her sweet face behind the soft, white clouds, like a blushing bride behind her white veil. What a glamour there was over land and sea as they walked silently along under the mellow moonbeams, listening to the musical murmur of the sighing waves. Suddenly Frederick Thornton stood still, looking down into the lovely face, his hand involuntarily closing and holding prisoner the little trembling one that lay on his arm. "You asked me why I risked my life to says yours. I will answer you now. It was because I love you with all my heart, with all my soul. Without you, life would be a blank; with you, it would be a paradise. I love you with the strongest love man ever felt for woman—a love that would brave all dangers to win you. You told me out on the water that you—" The sentence never was finished. Doris turned upon him like a flash. " Your love ! " she panted. "Heaven help the woman who believes in it. It is as false and cruel as death itself. Hush ! Not another word. I will not hear it. Never speak to me again. I would put the whole world between us if I could. In daring to speak to me of love, you have can- celled the debt of gratitude I owed you." Before Frederick Thornton could find his voice to reply, she had fled. He found himself stand- ing alone, lost in a maze of bewilderment on the beach. "Am I mad, or do I dream?" he cried, hoarsely. "My love—an insult! What can she mean ?" Then suddenly a strange light seemed to break in upon him. He was Banker Thornton's son, and heir to a million at his father's death; but in his own right at present he had but a moderate allow- ance, while Miss Fielding was already an heiress in her own right. "Did she think I meant to woo and win her for the sake of her wealth?" Anger and wounded pride came to his rescue, blunting the saw,'s of her words. If there was one class of Inca he had always detested above others it was fortune-hunters. And the thought that he should be classed as one of those despicable creatures cut to his heart like the sharp thrust of a dagger. The next morning the deplorable news was circu- lated among the young ladies that Mr. Thornton had left the hotel the night before. "Oh, how provoking !" they chorused in a breath. "And the season at its height, too. How we shall miss him at the hops ! He was a charm- ing gallant. How provokin4 that the attraction was not strong enough to keep him here to the end of the season.' And more than one glance was maliciously turned toward Doris. Doris turned quietly to the. pretty blonde who had made the remark. "Perhaps he went because the attraction else- where was strongest—as it should be in his case. I believe Nlr. Thornton to—be—married." "Married ?" echoed the little group, in amaze- ment. "Surely that cannot be, Miss Fielding. What reason have you for thinking so, and who is the lady ?" "Some three years ago he was betrothed to Miss Vivian Courtney—and I have every reason to believe—married her," returned Dork in a low, faint voice. "Indeed you are mistaken," declared one of the group, briskly. "He was engaged to. Miss Court- ney, it is quite true, but for some unexplained reason, the marriage was broken off. He went abroad, and about that time her father died of a fit of apoplexy. A year later, after waiting in vain for her handsome lover to return and make up their quarrel, Vivian married a wealthy sea captain for his gad. They had anything but a happy life of it, and at last he died, and his young widow is spending the money as last as she can. I read in one of the society journals she was ex- pected here this season. No doubt she has heard that her old lover is here, and is following him up, And that handsome Frederick Thornton has taken French leave." Doris listened like one turned suddenly to stone. The long porch with its groups of promenaders, the white beach and the long stretch of restless sea beyond, seemed to whirl around her. An, Heaven had she heard aright, or was this a cruel mockery of the senses? Vivian and Frederick had parted— three—years—ago? Ah, surely it could not have been! They loved each other too well for that. And believing himself free to woo and win Vivian, what had come between them? Could it be that his conscience had smitten him when he came face to face that night with the poor child-bride whom he had married only to desert, and did remorse overcome him with the knowledge she had sought death to set him free? And was it Heaven's retribution upon him, she wondered, that he should meet her again, and know- ing her not,—she was so changed in name, face and fortune—fall desperately in love with her? That he did love her now, she could not doubt! Had he not risked his life for her? Was there ever a stronger test of love than that? And she had sent him away—oh, cruel, cruel! 4141 i *',ri'v 91 Oi:•.t qther Doris canc.' out

to her for Yengeance ! He must suffer as she had suffered. He must feel, pang for pang, the cruel torture of unrequited love, such as she had felt in the horror or that never-to-be-for.:otten hour when kindly strangers, pitying her youth and her friend- lessness, had broken the heartrending truth to her —that he had forsaken her.
CHAPTER XXX. PARTED AGAIN.

"WHEN I forget the past, then I will forgive him —never until then," Doris thought, bitterly. She tried to take up the old life again ' • tried to be as happy as she was before Frederick Thointen crossed her path for the second time. But it was a task beyond her accomplishment. A voice was for ever crying out to her : "You have won his love at last. Why did you break his heart and your own too, by sending him

away from you?" _ The thought that poor, hapless Doris of the past was avenged brought her DO comfort. Should she write to him and recall him? He was still her husband; yes, her husband! Her heart thrilled
at the thought. "No, no, she would not recall him. Her pride rebelled against this. He should not have gone

away so hastily." The following week, among the new arrivals, came the charming young widow, Vivian Carsdale. That evening, for the first time since that cruel event which had happened three long years before, Vivian and Doris met again face to face. Vivian turned a ghastly white, even under her plentiful supply of rouge. "Who is that young girl ?" she asked one of the ladies standing near, and indicating Doris. "That? Why, Miss Fielding—the belle of New- port l" returned her companion, gazing admiringly after Doris's tall, slim, graceful figure. "Why, how white you look, Mrs. Carsdale I What can be the matter? You look as if you had seen a ghost." "I almost imagine I have," retorted Vivian, turning abruptly away. "Was there ever a face so like?" muttered
Vivian, when ehe found herself aione in her own boudoir. "If I did not know that Doris was
sleeping under the waves, I should say that the girl is Doris, old, and grown taller, with the same features, yet a thousand times more beautiful."

. She took great care to place herself near Doris the next day, where she could listen to her voice, observe every play of those mobile features; an again it struck Vivian as to how like this girl's voice was to that of Doris. In that same hour these two, whose paths had crossed each other so strangely, were presented to

each other. _ _ "You remind me so strangely of one whom I used to know," said Vivian, sweetly, "that. do you know, I am almost lost in wonder sometimes, the similarity is so striking." She was watching Doris narrowly, and saw the flush and the look of confusion that crossed her lovely face. The more Vivian talked to Miss Fielding, the more a certain wild idea that had taken possession of her became strengthened in her mind. Very ingeniously Vivian led the conversation around to education. "Where were you educated, Miss Fielding ?" she asked, suddenly. And almost instantly, without stopping to think, Doris had uttered the fatal words that sprang to
her lips: "At Madame Delmar's seminary, Beech Grove,

Maryland." Vivian uttered a little stifling scream. All her doubts now verged into assurances. With lightning. like rapidity, she turned upon the shrinking girl before her. No change of appearance, nothing in this world, could have veiled Doris's indentit y from the rival who had hated her with such a bitter hatred three long years ago. "I know you. You cannot deceive me," she cried, shrilly. "You are Doris Brandon, ie girl who stole my lover from me, because I trusted you to deliver a letter to him. You are not dead, then. You have risen from the grave to come between us again. Now that I think of it, the body supposed to have been drowned was never found. Why are you here sailing under false colours? Miss Fielding, indeed! You shall be denounced as an impostor before to-morrow's sun rises." , Like a whirlwind, she turned and left Doris standing stunned, dazed, bewildered, on the sunlit veranda. Like one suddenly stricken blind, she slowly groped her way to her own room. "What did Vivian intend to do ? " she asked herself, with a great gasping sob. Had it been such a terrible sin, when in a frantic moment she had flung herself into the water? She knew how bitterly such an action would be condemned—that the verdict of the world would be—No matter how hard she had found life, she should have taken up her cross with patience and

resignation. This, then, was what Vivian meant; and more, having been saved from a watery grave, she shou!cl have let the fact become known. What if, believ- ing her dead, Frederick Thornton had married again? He would have been innocent of all wrong, and she would have had to answer for it. She could see now that it had been all wrong, keeping the fact that she still lived from her husband. That he did not love her was no excuse. She saw it all now in quite a different light from that in which she had ever thought of it before. What a sensation there would be on the morrow, when Vivian revealed all. All the world would know that she was a forsaken bride; that the man She had married had deserted her at the very altar. And they would say, too, that, in after years, when the child-bride (whom he had married so hastily, repenting of the rash deed even while the solemn marriage service was being uttered) was changed beyond recognition, she threw herself in his way under an assumed name, won his love, and trampled it under her feet. This lad been her plan of vengeance, and a most ignoble vengeance it had been. . "Yes, they would say all that of me !" moaned Doris, "and I could never endure that." Sooner or later the story would reach Frederick Thornton's ears, and, oh, how shocked he would be.

"Better that he should hear this from me than from the lips of a stranger," muttered Doris, pacing excitedly up and down her room, wringing her hands. Yes, yes, I will write to him, confessing ill; then I will go away so far he can never find me."

Seating herself before her writing-desk, with trembling hand and face as white as death, she began her letter to Frederick Thornton. It was a long, closely-written letter, blotted with tears. In it, she went back to that fatal night when she followed him and Vivian through the grounds of the villa, and had suddenly sprung out before them, throwing off her disguise, crying out that she, his mother's companion, was the bride he bad wedded, only to cruelly desert. And how, in the intense excitement of the moment, she had turned from him, without wait- ing to hear one word of defence, if he had any to make for such an action, and had flung herself Into the river. How she had been saved from death, and had made her way to New York, where the accident befell her from which Karl Lancaster was instrumental in rescuing her. She also told him of the great discovery that had ensued—that she, the poor little dependent, who had suffered all the pangs of poverty, was an heiress—the daughter of Hulbert Brandon Field- ing, an English milord. She told how the impulse to confess who she was had been strong upon her when, after an absence of three long years, she had suddenly met him abroad that day. And how, seeing he did not recognise her, because she had changed so greatly during the length of time that had intervened, she had made up her mind never to reveal her identity, come what might. Also of the idea that had taken possession of her that, loving Vivian as he had loved her in the past, and believing himself free, no doubt he had wedded her. She had been of this opinion when they were talking together out .on the sands on that night he left Newport so suddenly. She then told of her subsequent discovery that he had parted from Vivian for ever on that fatal Digiit three years ago; and of Vivian's arrival at the hotel, and how she had recognised her, declar- ing I hat on the morrow the whole world should know het story. "I could never endure that," she wrote, piteously, "and so lam going away—going so far thitt no one who has ever looked upon my face will ever behold. me "Vivian accuses me of endeavouring to come between you and her again. This I earnestly, solemnly declare is untrue. It is this which sends me into exile. Another year this could bo done, but not at the present meeting.
UNOPPOSED OFFICERS.

The CHAIRMAN announced that Mr. S. E. Warren had been nominated secretary. Mr. T. Pemberton, treAsurer, and Messrs. Webster and T. Wallington, auditors. As these were the only nominations for these offices, these gentlemen were elected unanimously.
THE PRESIDENT.

The CrtainuAN said that they would all knew that he had been president for three years, arid he must say that he had done his best in that position. (Applause.) He might not have pleased everybody but that was not in man's power in this life. It had been a great experience to him to be president of the Rugby Football glut). as he had been able to study so many phases of human nature. As he was about to be shelved he would like to say a few words. He had been a footballer himself at one time, and he always thought he should like to be "cock of „e walk." He had hoped that while he had been president Warrington would have been at the top of Rugby competition. Of course he had been "dished," and he had not lived to be president when Warrington was at the top of the tree, latit he had no doubt that some president would see that. He wanted Rugby foot- ball to flourish, he did not want the Association code to get the better of it. He paid a tribute to the committee with whom he had worked for the way in which they had conducted their business, and said that he had always the best interests of the club at hear. He also claimed to have done something to promote Rugby foot- ball in Warrington by the local competitions. (Applause.) They would find players to-day in Warrington first team wno possibly would not have been prominent footballers but for these competitions. (Applause.) He had also done them a good turn by asking their worthy Mayor to be president of the club for the ensuing year. (Ap- plause.) He thought it would be a great benefit to the club, to have the chief magistrate of the town at their head, and he was glad thatthe Mayor very readily con- sented to hold the office. He proposed that the Mayor be president for the ensuing twelve months. . .
Air. HARRY TOFT seconded the motion which was heartily carried.
THANES TO THE HET! RING ERESIDENT.

Mr. D. TINNION moved a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Davies for his services to the club during his three years presidency. He spoke in high terms of the way in which Mr. Davies had acted, and thought him to be the best president they had ever had. Mr. T. WALLINGTON seconded, and said that Mr. Davies' genial face and happy disposition had done much to smooth the meetings which he had attended. The resolution was carried unanimously, and Mr. Davies briefly responded.

THANKS TO THE REPORTERS. Mr. T. WALLINGTON said that they would notice on the balance sheet the sum of £2 Os. 41. for reporting last season's matches. There was a saving of £l5 upon the previous year. He thought that the committee had been very wise in their decision to give the work to the work- ing reporters of the town. The persons who had under- taken this work were members of the Institute of Journalists, and he thought that the best thanks of the club were due to those friends who had so kindly under- taken the work for the benefit of the club. The re- porters as far as he could see had been very accurate in their reports,which they had given with very much de- tail. He thought that with that, and for saving the club £l5, they deserved their hearty thanks. Mr. DATIES seconded the resolution and endorsed what Mr. Wallington had said. He said that he did not know of any town in Lancashire where reporters had stood by the club so well. The resolution was carried unanimously, and Mr. C. lirow, replying on behalf of the reporters, said that they had experienced great pleasure in doing the work for the club, and they had a real personal feeling for the club, instead of looking at the work as previously from the hardwork point of view. div.p: A GENEROUS INTERVIEW.
TRUTH STRINGER THAN FICTION.

A REPORTER writes in the " Berwick Advertiser " • After having interviewed Mr. George Jaffrie, of Leit- holme, Berwiek-on-Tweed, I must frankly admit that his is a case which very aptly exemplifies the well- 'known adage, that" truth is stranger than action." Mr. Jaffrie would have personally crefer el that his experience should not be reported in the newspapers, but he generously set aside his own preferences and agreed to allow this interview to be published for the sake of other sufferers. He said, " It is seven years past in July since 1. was taken ill. At that time I was seized with a severe pain in the stomach, and was treated by a very painstaking and skilful physician.; but it was not many days before was confined to bed, the doctor attending me for about eight months. I got gradually worse, and the doctor gave me entirely up, and said that I was incurable. He said that I was only heaping up expense, and that there was no medical man who could do me any good. H e said that my lungs were bad, and that my heart was bad, that the bladder was bad, and that the kidneys were bad. In fact, I was all bad. After that, I tried corresponding WITH LONDON DOCTORS,

and they were of opinion that I was suffering from rheumatism in the stomach and kidneys—but finding that I was making no headway, I gave up hope. I never thought that I would be out of bed again. Another very clever doctor whom I consulted declined to take up my case. The doctors evidently gave ma Al p, and everybody in the village of Leitholm knows this. In the depth of my despair I was persuaded to try a new medicine that had effected Some extraordinary cures, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People—and to my intense gratitude they, in a very short time, began to pull me together, and made a new man of me." " When did you begin taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills?"
" About the end of last May. I perceived an improve- ment in a short time, and after I had taken about twelve of the small boxes,

FOUND A GREAT DIFFERENCE. I have continued taking the Pills, and the cure has been gradual but steady. For about threo years orevious to the time I began to take Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People I was never off my back, and HAD TO BE HELD UP IN BED TO CHANGE MY SHIRT. Now I am able to walk about the house. In good weather I can go out every day. it first people in the village would not believe that I was able to be out until they saw me." The above, concludes the" 13erwick Advertiser," are the absolute and proved fapts of what is certainly a most marvellous cure, and there is not thu least possibility that any exaggeration can have crept in. Our representative saw Mr. Jaffrie, and satisfied himself of his condition, and the truth of his interest- ing and convincing narrative. He saw also, and spoke with, Mr. Jaffrie's fellow villagers, who knew of his crippled and, to ill human knowledge, helplesB condition. There is no question as to how this extraordinary cure has been effected. Dr. Williams' Pink rills are an unfailing cure for rheumatism, neural- gia, paralysis, locomotor ataxy, St. Vitus' dance, nervous headache, and prostration; also diseases of the blood, such as scrofula, chronic erysipelas, /sc. They are a splendid tonic, and restore pale and sallow complexions to the glow of health, a specific for all troubles peculiar to the female sex, and in men cure all diseases arising from worry, overwork, or excesses of whatever nature.

Trig Pills are sold by all chemists, or may he had direct from Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, of 46, Holborn- viaduct, London, at 2s. 9d. a box, or six boxes for 13.4. 9d. ANNUAL MEETING OF THE LOCAL BRANCH.

Oa Thursday last week the annual meeting of the Warrington branch of the above Society was held in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall,the use of which had been granted by the Mayor. There was a good attend- ance, and amongst those present were the Mayor and Mayoress, &Merman and Mrs. E. Greenall, (the latter, treasurer), Mrs. J. Harrison, Mrs. Slater, Mrs. Broad- bent, Miss Broadbent, Miss Silvia Broadbent, the Misses Riminer, Mr. William Long, Mr. T. Birchall, Mrs. H. Wood, Miss Long, Mr. J. D. Buckton, Miss Bessie Dutton and Mr. Rodger (of Moore), Mr. C. n. Broadbent, Mr. and Mrs. C. L. Evans, Inspec- tor McAteer (local officer), and Mr. W. B. Greener (sec.). The chair was taken by the Mayor, who was accom- panied on the platform by the Rev. Benjamin Waugh (non. director of the So..•,i.ty), and Mr. Greener (local hon. sec.).

div.head: WORE IN TIIIi WARRINGTON DISTRICT.
div.p: WORE IN TIIIi WARRINGTON DISTRICT.

The first business of the meeting was the reading by the secretary of the third report of the Warrington and District branch of the Society. The repart stated that ' "Another year of the Society's work in Warrington and district vias completed on the 31st of March, and the committee present to all interested in the children's cause the third annual report. The past year has been an exceptionally busy one, and adds overwhelming evid- ence of the need of the Society in our midst, and has given many striking indications of the benefits and bless- ings its action has conferred on the suffering children in this district. Our officer has investigated 152 cases, and these involve the welfare of 578 children of whom 298 are boys and 280 girls. The complaints are classified under the following heads :—Gmeral ill-treatment, 4 ; assault, 5; neglect and starvation, 142; begging cases, 1. The cases were disposed of as follows :—Warned, 93 ; pro,:lecuted, 57 ; otherwise dealt with, 2. Number of cases investigated at different places :—Warrington, 65 ; Widnes, 47 ; Runcorn, 15 ; Lymm, 6 ; Altrincham, 4 ; Sale, 3 ; Latchford, 3 ; Grolborne, 6 ; St. Helens, 2 ; Prescot, 1. Number of children insured, 195; total amount of insurance £506 23. 61 The total imprison- ment inflicted during the year is twelve years and three weeks. Toe Inspector's report of the result of super- vision of these cases shows a general improvement and the beginning of happier lives, both for the children themselves and for the parents who were punished. We regret to say the prosecutions have been very numerous, but we were bound to undertake them, as the evildoers would not become amenable to the kindly advice of our officer, or take any heed of the " warning notice " served on them. lii the many cases where a drunken woman rules the house nothing has any effect but im- prisonment. We have to point out that 86 per cent, of the cases are due to drunkenness :—Fifty-six per cent.to drunken mothers; 10 per cent, to drunken fathers; 20 per cent, to drunken fathers and mothers. During the year further steps have been taken to widen the influ- ence of the society in our district, and to secure at the same time more financial. support. . _

LYMM.--rhrongh the kindness of our friends in Lymm a meeting was arranged, and Mr. Waugh came down and formed a District Committee, and through the energy of our district correspondent and others our funds have been substantially helped. RUNCORN.—Lady Brooke kindly arranged for and con- vened a drawing-room meeting at Norton Priory in the autumn, at which Mr. Waugh gave an 'address, and a District Committee was formed. TrINANCES.—We have to congratulate ourselves that through the interest and liberality of our friends we are able to meet our expenditure and hand £64 16s. 41. over to the National Society to help to extend the work in poor districts yet out of reach through lack of funds. The tot il income was £361 17s. 4d. and the expenditure £297 Is. which leaves the above balance. In conclusion, we would express our thanks to the police generally for the ready co-operation and assist- ance afforded to the Society's Inspector, and to each and all of tho4e who have assisted in carrying out the great work we have at heart. We feel it is due to our officer to place on record our appreciation of the manner in which he has discharged his duties. We look forward with hope to the future, and commend the work to all, and ask their continued practical sympathy; we appeal in the name of the little ones whose wail cannot reach the ears of those best able to help them. We ask not for means to place them in ideal circumstances, but simply such continued support as will enable us to /rave justice done to them at the hands of those whose duty it is to mete it out to them."—This report was signed by George Rodger, chairman; Mrs. Edward Greenall, hon. treasurer; W. B. Greener, hon. secretary. Mr. Wm/Jam LONG proposed the adoption of the report and said that they must all have a feeling of gratitude to those ladies and gentlemen who had taken such an active interest in the work of the Society in introducing it into this neighbourhood which, he thought, though perhaps not more than other great centres of population, needed the work of such a Society as this. It was a Fad point that the greatest number of cases of cruelty arose through the drunkenness of the parents, and he hoped that the action of this Society, working splendidly as it was, might have a corrective effect in the end and bring about a happier state of things. The Rev. W. 11. DRUMMOND seconded the motion, and said that he thought the tenor of the report gave them every reason to have full confidence in the executive committee who had charge of the work in Warrington. It exercised a great deal ot discrimination, patience, and discretion as to the action which was taken. -The most appalling fact was the number of eases which had come before the committee during the past year,of cruelty to children, owing to drunken mothers, and that was one of the sad features of the social life in our large towns at the present time. It used to be considered the privilege of a man to get drunk and that was bad enough, but it was all up with the home when the mether took to this habit. The Society would be doing a direct good to the children by bringing these cases before the maeistrates or by warning the mothers sufficiently to make them reform, and he knew that it was perfectly true that very strong steps indeed had to be taken when the drink curse had entered into a home in that form. Good would be done in bringing prominently before the public this terrible fact that drunkenness among women was a dread reality and he feareo was growing in our large towns and the sooner we woke up to that fact and took counsel together the better it would be. The speaker hoped the time would come when there would be restored to society that deep respect of child life which was an essential part of true Christianity. (Rear, hear.) The motion was then put to the meeting and carried. The MAYOR said that as he considered the Society was doing a good work in Warrington he was glad to see such a good renre.entation of the people belonging to the Society there that night. Ile had pleasure in intro- ducing Mr. Wangh. "'KR WAUGH'S ADDRRSS.

-- The Rev. RRNJAMIN WAUGH (hon. director of the observed that his object was to speak of the history of the Society. Eleven years ago the name of the Societr had never been uttered in the English tongue, nor did it seemed to have bean dreamed even by ;the English people that the child had *rights. Th.r might search 'English literature of all kinds up to 10 years ago and they would find that the sacredness of child-life had not been uttered on a platform, not been uttered in a pulpit, nor been uttered in Parliament as a political theme. Six years ago Parliament passed what is known as tbe Children's Charter, and that laid down totally new tenets in English law, and in the main par- ticular and at the bottom of the whole was the rights of child. The speaker mentioned that they had done a great deal in punishment and they had sent some 7,000 or 8.000 fathers and mo'hers to gaol for terms of im- prisonment, but the punishinrnt thy had inflicted had done comnaratively no good compared with the educa- tion that they had given. People said 80 per cent, of the ernelties in Warrington were through drunkenness, but in some countries in England. the nropertion rose to 90 per cent., and in nthers sank to 40 per cent. He could !nap out kngland and conjecture the number of public houses they had for the populatism, without going ints the towns. simply by means of the returns of the officers of the Society. Violence was less common where drunkenness was not the great cause and more common where it was. The average wage in cases of imprisonment had been Ll 7s. Bd. per week, or 53. higher than the average wage of the country, and in every case sent to prison for penal servitude the average was over £2. Some people had said it was ignorance that caused cruelty to children and he had classified 186,000 cases and found that ignorance had little or nothint, to do:with it. One of the last and worst cases he had had to deal with was the head of a college ; most of the offenders had an average English education, not high, but equal to the standard of the country. Some- times it was said that the cruelty arose through large families but he contended that it was the small families and not the large in which cruelty to children existed, taken on the whole It was a striking fact that they had not sent a man to roffial servitude with seven children. Alluding to financial matters Mr. Waugh said that 11 years ago the income of the society was £3OO and to-day it was £54500. Eleven years ago it was said the society was not needed, and last Satdiday her Majesty gave them a Royal Charter which made them one of the permanent institntions of this country. At first it was deemed impossible to cause Parliament to pass a statute on behalf of children and yet they had lately massed a second. They were now realizing that this new advent, this new idea, about a child was a great and grand thing and a movement which was rapidly pro- gressing. Referring to child-life irsurance, the speaker remarked that a great deal had been said on that sub- ject, some of which he sympathised with and some he did not. They had 71.000 children neglected and out of ,that number 21.100 were insured for £5. Not one of the children nerrlerted wilfnlly and insured was insured in wnrkingttens' own (luta, such as the Foresters, the Oddfellows. or the Druids. All were insured in com- mercial sncieties which had collectors going round from door to door touting, and in which there was nothing done except on a purely commercial business. It led to this ennrinsi,,n that the rules of the friendly societies were sufficient to secure children from the dangers of child-life insurance, for nut f 21,000 cases that had not one concern ed with a friencliv society. In conclu- sion, the rev. gentleman said that he wanted them to realize that their work was by all means a charitable work. Their action in the past bad justified everything

div.p: they had said, and after they had carried on:their crusade for the next 10 years there would be a new genera Von of thinkers, and instead of fathers and mothers thinking i right to starve baby and let it die and have a little funeral and big drink they would give the baby its natural chance to secure its place deep in their hearts. The speaker finished up with the declama- tion, England suffered not through drink but through politics and the sooner we got rid:of:these quarrels and ceased sparring and cockfighting. in Parliament, and backing of one party against another, the better. . .

The MAYOR proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Waugh for his very interesting address. Miss BESSIE DUTTON seconded, and said they were glad Mr. Waugh was so enthusiastic, and she would be glad to always second a vote of thanks to anyone who had enthusiasm in such a good cause. That was what they liked—real enthusiasm. It was dying out in reli- gion and in many places whet.," it might be exercised to advantage. (Hear, hear.) The vote was accorded unanimously. Mr. WAUGH, in responding, answered two questions by saying that the society had no homes of any kind, as it only sought to improve homes and not to break them up, and to see that children lived endurable lives with their fathers and mothers. The other answer was that in the society there was no denomination ; it was abso- lutely unsectarian. He concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding. This motion was carried, on being seconded by Mr. Rodger, and the MAYOR, in reply, said that he would be pleased to assist Mr. Greener any time to further the object of the society. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: LAMENTABLE SUICIDE OF A WA RRINGTON MAN. "DRIVEN" TO DEATH.
div.p: LAMENTABLE SUICIDE OF A WA RRINGTON MAN. "DRIVEN" TO DEATH.

On Friday morning about 6 a.m ,Thomas Hughes a man who was working on a pontoon near the cantilever bridge, Latchford, noticed the body of a man floating upright in the Ship Canal. The body was secured and towed to the locks where the water was raised and the body taken out. P.C. Millington was communicated with and had the body washed and taken to the Dog and Dart" inn. In deceased's coat was found a pocket-book with the following sad note " My name is Peter Higham, ot Battersby-lane, Warrington. Tell my brother I hope he will forgive me but I was driven to it all through my foolish actions; and tell my 'sister lam very sorry for what I have done but I could not help it.' P.C, Millington made enquiries and found that deceased was aged 20 and had been lodging at 22, Battersby-lane with a Mrs. Harrison. On Sunday night the sth,deceased went out and got some drink and on the Monday and Tuesday was ill. On the evening of the latter day, after com- plaining of pains in his head, he went out and pledged a waistcoat, and nothing more was known of him until the finding of his body.

div.head: PRIAIRCTSE LEAGUE. ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON HABITATION.
div.p: THE PRIAIRCTSE LEAGUE. ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON HABITATION.

The annual meeting-oithe members of the Warrington Habitation of the Primrose League was held on Thursday last week in the Assenahly Rooms of the Conservative Club, there being a good attendance. Mrs. Reynolds, the Ruling Councillor, presided, and amongst those present were Mr. John White. Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. G. Pilling, Mr. and Mrs. R. Isherwood, Mr. Truslove, Councillor and Mrs. Smethurst, Mr. J. H. Smethurst, Alderman and Mrs. Francomb, Councillor Bennett, Mr. John Roberts, Mr. H. J. Westbrook, Mrs. R. Johnson, Miss I. Reynolds, Mr. L. A. Voisey (hon. treasurer), Mr. C. H. Wood (hon. secretary), &c. Votes of thanks were passed to Mrs. Reynolds and the officers of the habitation for their services during the year. Alderman FRANCOMB moved that the following consti- tute the Council for the ensuing year :—Mrs. Joseph Harrison, Mrs. J. Grounds, Mrs. R. Johnson, Miss Reynolds, Miss Voisey, Messrs. J. Coxos, James Smet- hurst, John Roberts, R. Woods, George Pilling, Ralph Johnson, R. H. Dainteth and L. A. Voisey hon. treasurer, C. H. Wood hon. secretarv.—Mr. Armstrong seconded, and the motion was agreed to. Mr. Josti ROBERTS moved the re-election of the wardens as follows;—Town Hall ward, Mrs. James Smethurst; Whitecross ward, Mrs. Ralph Johnson; Bewsey ward, Miss Atherton; Orford ward, Mrs. Gandy; Fairfield ward, Mrs. Gibson; Howley ward, Miss Reynolds; St. Austin's ward, Miss Voisey ; Latchford ward, Mrs. Grounds. —Mr. J. Battersby seconded the motion, and it was carried.—This concluded the business meeting:.
A public meeting in connection with the Habitation was then held. Mr. Rnbert Davies prosiding.

The CHAIRMAN again referred to' the absence of Mr. Pierpoint. He remarked that since Mr. Pierpoint was elected member for the borough he had closely attended to the requirements of the borough in Parliament. (Hear, hear.) He was not afraid of opening his mouth in the House on questions which nailed for it, but he did not weary it by useless orations upon fads of different kinds. He was now engaged on a select committee, 1 which was a great honour, due no doubt to Warrington being interested in the file trade. But with such a Government, and such a heterogeneous mass of sup- porters as this Government had, it was no wonder that they felt a great interest in the coming contest. Let them considet for a moment what this Government was doing,and it there were anv gentle- men belonging to the Warrington Angling Association present he thought they would understand the simil Rude which he was about to utter. They talked about "filling the cur and "ploughing the sand" but he said they were doing what fishermen did—they were baiting the hole expecting a big catch at the next general election. (Laughter and applause.) He thought they would be very much disappointed. (Hear, hear.) Let them look at the various baits they were laying. First of all, they had to give a bait to the Irish. They had 103 members of that nation in the House of Commons, 71 of whom were Home Rulers, and it was not too much to say that these 71 were really the standing support against which the Ministry always had to lean. (Hear, hear.) History recorded that there was a Richard Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick, who was called the Kingmaker, but he (Mr. Davies) called these 71 Home Rulers, Cabinet makers. (Laughter and applause.) Addresses were also given by Mr. John White, Alder- men Franeomb, and others.

div.head: DEVELOPMENT OF ELECTRECITY.
div.p: THE DEVELOPMENT OF ELECTRECITY.
STEAM RAILWAYS DOOMED.

Mr. Preece, C. 8., the electrician to the Post Office— surely a practical expert if there ever was one—has re- cently enumerated some instances of the development of electricity that would seem incredible did they come from a less authoritative source. Mr.Preece tells us that, having demonstrated over and over again the possibi- lity of sending messages through some miles of wireless space, he at length has been able to put his discoveries to a practical test. "A few days ago," he says, " the cable which runs from Oban to the Island of Mull got out of order. Connection by induction was effected across the Sound of Mull at the narrowest part,which is about two miles wide." A person now signing a cheque, say in Paris, can have the signature simultaneously re- produced in London. To watch the movements of a pen guided by an invisible hand, as the writer recently did, is calculated to make even a strong-nerved person ex- tremely uncomfortable. When the merits of that extremely sensitive instru- ment the thermopole come to be more generally recog- nised, the doctors at a fever hospital sitting in their offices will receive instant intelligence of any rise in the temperature of patients. The thermopole was used when Sir W. Harcourt's son was lying ill with typhoid at the Treasury. One night the temperature nearly reached 105 degrees. The watchful little instrument instantly flashed the rise through the wire to the doctor's house, arousing the sleeper,who was in his patient's room with- in half-an-hour. It will probably sound fantastic, if not absurd,to talk about the odours of sweet-smelling flowers being electri- cally transmitted, but the statement is made in all sober earnes'ness. It has not been accomplished yet,but doubt- less will be. It is also now reported that the development of elec- tric railways in America is beginning to revolutionise travel. The steam railways are finding it difficult to compete with the electric trolley lines over large parts of New England. An electric line is also projected to connect Haverhill, in Massachusetts, with Quebec, in Canada, a distance of 280 miles. The Cincinnati, Hamilton, and Drayton Railway, one of the older America lines: is about to substitute electricity for steam power. The competition of the electric trolley lines has brought down the fares on the Philadelphia and Reading, and is expected to do so on the Penn- sylvania Railway. And, finally, the greatest project of all, the Inter-Oceanic Electric Railway, has been incor- porated in Illinois with a capital of 200,000,000d015. It will construct an elevated electric railway between Chicago and New York, and finally from Chicago to the Pacific. American engineers seem to be all agreed that steam railwaya are doomed within a quarter of a cen- tury, so far as America is concerned.

div.head: AN IMAGINARY NAVAL ENCOUNTER,
div.p: AN IMAGINARY NAVAL ENCOUNTER,
"OCEAN HAWKS" IN THE ATLANTIC.

The conditions of modern naval warfare are portrayed in a lively fashion by an imaginative writer in an American contemporary. It seems our ingenious cousins have in their possession two warships f a terrible type. They are called" the triple-screw commerce-des- troyers" and are said to be able to run down the fastest ocean liners. Their mission is to capture the merchant vessels of an enemy. locidsntally, they would fight if put to it but their vocation is the destruction of unarmed Americans are nothing if not boastful; and it is not surprising that possessing two such formidable craft and a few rusty war tubs, they should he jubilant and inclined to let their neighbours know what they have to expect should they summon this mighty flotilla from their New York anchorage. having supposed war to have been declared between Great Britain and America the writer proceeds to sketch an imaginary encounter between one of our ocean grey- hounds, the "Campania," and their ship the "Columbia." The first endeavour of the enemy would be to prevent us getting food supplies from Canada, all the American ports being closed against us. Tres writer assumes that Hallifax would be the point for which we should make.

Knowing then the probable route of our merchant steamers, one of the new "commerce destroyers" would be sent in search. Reaching a spot in mid-ocean, approximately on the track of the ships she sought, the " Columbia " would steam back and forth on a meridian of longitude, covering a range of perhaps thirty knots on each course, at a fifteen-knot speed, keeping the sharpest kind of a look•out all the time. Having a range of vision in clear weather of at least fifteen miles, she would be almost sure to sight the enemy, if the latter passed in the daytime. Assume, then, that the " Campania " were sighted in the forenoon, at a distance of fifteen miles, and that the "Campania" were equally quick to spy the "Colum- bia." Probably neither would be able to recognise the other accurately beyond a greater distance than ten miles. The "Columbia," having the heels of everything, would run straight towards the stranger, but the " Cam- pania " would not change her course until she suspected the " Columbia " to be a f ag. At the first glimpse of another steamer the " Colum- bia " would spread the banked fires under all the reserve boilers, would put on the forced draught and start all three engines at work. By the time the " Campania " had taken alarm and changed her course in flight the " Columbia's " three screws would be revolving at their highest speed, the ship would be stripped for action, and the long, stern chase would have begun. Let us assume, as the writer does, that ten miles separate the two ships, and that each is in a condition capable of doing her best. We now give the results in the author's own words.

" On board the" Columbia " there is no excitement, save such as naturally accompanies the exertion to its full capacity of enormous power. Furnaces are at white heat, while half naked firemen methodically shovel in additional fuel, and the great fans whirr incessantly as the air is driven into the fire-rooms and is sucked up through the glowing grate bars. As the steam pressure touches 170 pounds in one set of boilers, the safety valve lifts, and on the deck a roar is heard like the rage of an imprisoned and tortured giant. From end to end the mighty hull rattles and quivers with the throbs of the propellers, sharper and more staccato-like as the bow plunges and the stern lifts to the moderate surface swell. It matters not what may be the directions of the breeze, the ship makes her own wind as her speed rises above twenty-two knots, and the showers of hot cinders sweep the decks abaft the smoke-stacks. " Every eve on deck is levelled at the distant steamer, now in full flight, dead ahead. There is no question as to her identity, for no ether craft likely to be in that neighbourhood could hold such tremendous speed. For distant though she is, the " Campania's " officers on look-out aloft have been able to recognise her distin- guishing features of rig, hull and smoke-stacks. The occasional gleam of foam glancing from her bow as she plunges into a wave shows that she, too, is going at no ordinary speed." And se the race continues. Each vessel exerts its utmost powers. If only the " Campania" can hold out till night-fall it is possible she may escape in the dark- ness. But no ! Her speed slackens towards noon,. and she is observed to be getting rid of superfluous cargo. ' Her condition is getting desperate. At length her com- mander resorts to a ruse to gain some advantage over his rival. The " catamaran "is launched, loaded with shell and a time-fuse, by which he hopes to retard the progress of the steadily approaching vessel. It is of no avail, however. The wily captain of the" Columbia" notices the act, and is suspicious. He alters his course a little, and a terrific explosion in his neighbourhood, shortly afterwards, tells him he has acted wisely. The struggle is now coming to a close. In vain is coal piled on atid more cargo thrown over board. The " Campania" slackens down considerably, and when within firing distance she makes a weak attempt at self- defence with her 61n. guns. But she is completely over- matched by the superior armament of her foe, and ulti- mately has to haul down her flag. She is first" winged and then bagged." Such is the picture presented to us ; and though doubt- less written to please a certain section of the American public, it points a moral from which we should not be slow to profit. But our enthusiastic contemporary has overlooked one point. lie is evidently unaware that we have already in course of construction two powerful cruisers,the first instalments of a tpye of vessel designe3 to hunt down ocean hawks like the " Columbia " and "Minneapolis." and that thelr mission will be to protect our liners in time of war.

div.head: WARRINGTON CORPORATION
div.p: WARRINGTON CORPORATION
BATHS. OPENING OF THE SEASON,
GRAND SWIMMING GALA.

The swimming season in Warrington commenced well c n Tuesday evening with the gala and polo match at the Baths, Legh-street. There was a good attendance, and the chair was taken by Councillor Percy Davies,and the hon. officials were :—Judges: Messrs. Derbyshire, Grace, Beswick and Toft ; handicappers, Messrs. Derby- shire and Grace; starter, Mr. Derbyshire ; check starter, Mr. T. Locker; referee, Mr. J. F. Finegan ; goal-scorers, Messrs. Grounds and Stredder. The programme did not show over-much variety but the events particularised were taken great interest in, and were also of import- ance.

The first item was the 50 yards youths' handicap, for which there were the following three prizes : Ist prize, gold medal ; 2nd prize, silver medal ; 3rd prize, bronze medal. There were two heats and three competitors in each, the first and second swimming in the final. This resulted in A. Ashton, J. Hampton, J. Hughes and L. Davies being pitted against each other for the medals, which were won by Ashton (first), Hughes (second) and Davies (third). In the two lengths maiden handicap the prizes were the same, but there were eight heats and about 30 com- petitors. The firsts only,swam in the final and the win- nine eight were F. Tyldesley,Diamond T.S.C.,S. Preston, V.S.C., F. Bailey, V.S.C., W. J. Coe,C.S.C., J. E. Moore, N.L.C., W. Creighton, W.S.C., R. Beattie and J. Ifilton. These competitors in the final all swam together and the race resulted in Beattie being declared first, Tyldesley second, and Hilton third. A 100 yards open handicap with the same number of heats was also swam off, seven of the ;heats being won by Preston (swim over), D. Moult, S.S.C., Lindley, 0.5. C., J. E. Moore, N.L.G., E. Robinson, N.H.S.C. (swim over), F. Garside, W.S.C., and J. Hilton, T.S.C. In heat 5, J. H. Tyers (amateur champion cf the world) was allowed a swim over, his appearance being greeted with loud cheers. Mr. Derbyshire then announced that in compliment to the Warrington club Tyers had decided to make an attempt to do a better performance than be had previously accomplished. The champion stood in the proud position of holding a greater number of championships and records than any other swimmer and was able to say with truth that he never saw the man , yet in an amateur competition and from a fair mark, , who could make him bite the dust. He is the holder of the world's record, amateur or professional,under record conditions, for 100 yards, and before his advent in the swimming world the time stood at 1 mm. 81-5 secs, but Tyers had gradually lowered this to 1 min 2 2-5 secs. Tyers then plunged in and using the double overhand stroke went through the water at a tremendous speed and at the end it was announced that he had lowered the record by one-fifth of a second so that it now stand. at 1 min. 2 1.5 secs., and 150 yards he had done in 28 2-5 secs, which made the world's record for that distance. The 100 yards final was left to Moult, Hindley, Robin- son, and Tyers, the latter starting 23 secs. after the word "go "and coming in after a most exciting struggle, first by a few inches only. Robinson was second, Moult third, and Hindley fourth, thus entitling them to the following prizes :-Ist prize, marble clock; 2nd prize, gold medal ; 3rd prize, gold centre medal; 4th prize, silver medal. Tyers also won the fast-time prize, which was a gold breastpin value £1 Is. Od.

THE POLO MATCH. The event to which paramount interest was attached was the first round of the Liverpool and District Water Polo Competition between Warrington and North Liver- pool Gymnasium. Speculation was rife as to what the homesters would accomplish under theirchange of team. The latter was composed as follows : goal J. F. Dixon ; left back, P. Furness; right back, S. Beaman; half back, G. A. Scotson ; left forward, W. Ashton ; centre for- ward T.Locker (captain), and right forward, F. Turner, North Liverpool Gymnasium :—Goal, Newby ; left back, J. Harrison ; right back, B. Barton ; half back, M. Stanhope ; left forward T. Cairns ; centre forward, A. Sisson ; right forward, E. Cryan. As the result of the toss-up the visitors decided to de- fend the deep end of the bath for the first half. At the commencement of hostilities Locker was first to the ball which was takenjdown to the visitors' goal and Scotson was soon to the fore with a good, but futile attempt at goal. Beaman was granted a foul and passing to Locker who returned to Turner the latter put in a good shot which was hpwever fisted out. A general melee ensued out of which Scotson secured, passed to Locker who was close to the goal and in a moment put the ball through the posts. On the re-start Locker, as in every other instance, seized the ball which was forced up, but the visiting forwards retaliated and Beaman was again fouled by Barton. From this advantage Beaman threw to Locker who transferred to Furness, and the latter put in a shOt which re-bounded from the posts into thei hands of Ashton who before the goal-keeper was aware of his proximity, scored the second goal. Even play afterwards ensued and after a neat bit of passing be- tween the Warrington backs the ball came into the hands of Beaman who worked his way down to the visitors end, only to be disarmed on the point of scoring. An- other foul gave Furness a free throw, but nothing resulted. Scotson was next in possession and passed to Turner who shot at goal, but the ball rebounding was seized by Locker who again scored from close quarters. Shots alter this were frequent but unsuccessful, and a rush was made by the visitors which gave Dixon a busy time of it, but he relieved finely. More fouls were made but nothing further scored, and at half time the was Warrington 3 goals, Liverpool nil. Locker again secured in the second half and passed to Scotson who transferring to Ashton,the latter was fouled. Neither side gained the advantage for some time,but the visitors played better in the shallow end. Scotson made a good shot at goal but only hit the posts. The gymnasts then pressed, and Furness and Turner were fortunate in relieving. Another opportunity appearing Locker again scored,the ball dislodging the top-bar in its passage. Strenuous efforts were made on the part of the visitors and Dixon was hard pressed more than once, but on the call of time Warrington were the winners of a hard fought game by 4 goals to nil.
