PRESENTATION TO PRE SECRETARY. The Caen-max said he would like to tell the Warring- ton Swimming Club what a pleasure it had been to him to be there that evening. He felt it a high honour to be chairman of such a gala as that, and he thought they would agree with him that there was no swimming club in England that had more facilities or more sympathy from its town than Warrington. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) To those who did not know cie would like to inform them that it was the Corporation Bath, which he thought was second to none in the country, and they were anxious to make as much use of it as possible, and therefore they met in a handsome manner the swim- ming club, to whom were granted several concessions as regarded the price of season tickets. There were also, he added, special facilities for boys. They were instructed in the art of swimming and he asked one and all who were present to do their best to promote the interests of the Warrington Swimming Club. He himself thought there was no more pleasurable exercise than swimming, an he would ask the club to promote the interests of the young people in Warrington in learning to swim in their young days, as they would never forget it. There was one more pleasurable duty he had to do and that was to present a medal for life- saving to their worthy secretary, Mr. D. Walsh, who on the 25th April rescued a youth named Mannering, who was drowning in the bath. He had great pleasure in presenting to Mr. Walsh the medal. (Loud applause.) A number of youthful members of the Osborne-street Swimming Club, Manchester, next gave an exhibition of the life-saving drill, in the most approved style. The following necessary evolution; were gone through on the outside of the bath and in the water —The best means of releasing oneself from the grip of a drowning person ; effecting a rescue; and assistiog a tired swimmer. The method of restoring an apparently drowned person was also shown. All these different motions the boys went through with praiseworthy skill and were carefully watched by the members of the Warrington club who intend entering a competition for this drill. The prizes were then distributed and the first gala of the season closed after a very successful exhibition.

div.p: WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.
MUSICAL EXAMINATION.

The annual examination of the members of the War- rington Training College in music was held by Sir John Stainer, on Friday. The individual examination wag held during the day, and the students collectively were taken at nicht. The pii?ce de resistance was Sterndale Bennett's " May Queen," and several iniscellaneous selections. The principal vocalists for the evening were Miss Emily Garliak, Miss Eva Morton and Miss Jane Williams, and Messrs. J. atidy, J. Parkinson and W. H. Wallington, while the male portion of the chorus was composed of members of various church and chapel choirs in the town. It may be said that the members of Warrington Training College have always stood high in the number of marks ob..iined at these annual exam• inations, and last night's performance showed no sign of deterioration. The pieces for examination in addition to the "May Queen" were a part song, Gentle Swallow" (Rogers), for first year students; vocal waltz, " Blow soft winds" (Charles Vincent), for second year students; and part song, "Now the wearied sun declin- ing" (R. F. Lloyd), by thearndents collectively. A solo, "The promise of life" (Cowen), was given by Miss Jane Williams, and an instrumental quartet,Allegro moderato, ' from quartet in E flat op. (Schubert), was also effectively given by Messrs. R. H. Puo-s-ii, E. H. Clare, 0. Johnson and H. Bond. Au orche,tra did good service during the evening, and consisted of Mr. G. H. Pearson, first violin; Mr. E. H. Clare, second violin ; Mr. B. Johnson, viola ; Mr. Henry Bond, violoncello; Mr. R. Whitfield, double bass; Mr. W. A. Wood, harmonium : and the principal (Rev. Morley Stevenson) pianoforte, and the conductor was Mr. W. S. Woods.

MUSIC LICENSE TRANSFERS AT WARRINGTON.

MAt the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, before Mr. John Fairclough and other magistrates, the follow- ing transfers of music licenses were applied for r—Peter Chrimes, Roebuck Hotel, from Frank Toft ; S:•rali L. Stafford, Smith's Arrns,Legh-street,from Samuel Jones ; Ernest Ellis. Lion Hotel, from Joseph Taylor,. deceased ; Thomas George Grounds, Volunteer Inn, Cockhedge,fiom John Hughes ; Stephen Stirrup,Queen's Hotel, Sankey-at. new application. Mr. Arthur Browne in applying on behalf of Mr. Ellis said that unfortunately as long a notice was required for the transfer of a music license from a deceased person as though it were a new license. He had served:notice upon the persons required, and he now applied for the transfer.—The Chief Constable said that he had no. objection to Mr. Ellis. _

Mr. Browne also aoplied on behalf of Mr. Stirrup of the Queen's Hotel. He said that this was a new applica- tion. The room in the house which would be used for dancing was 24 feet lodg, and 12 feet broad, and the roof was higher than the police court root. Mr. Stirrup did not want to have regular singing. He simply wished to have the license to protect himself.—The Chief Constable said that the previous tenant had applied for a music license and had been refused.—Mr. F. Monliii :- On what grounds p—The Chief Constable : There were no grounds stated.

Mrs. Stafford, and Messrs. Chrimes, and Grounds,. made their applications personally, and the Chief Con- stable said that he had no objection to raise to any of , these, they were all applications for the renewal of ' license held by the previous tenants. The magistrates decided to grant all the applications. with the exception of the Queen's Hotel.

THE WORK OF A ,WARRINGTON EVANGELIST. In connection with the anniversary services of the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Sunday Schostl, a lecture was - given in the Wesleyan- Church on Monday evening by the Rev. John G. Bennett, son of Mr. John Bennett, of Bewsey liall,upon the above subject,it being an account of his travels to and fro in Great Britain, as a con- nexional evangelist. There was a very good audience, and the chair was occupied by Councillor U. R therts, J. P.
The Rev. John Kirn having bricfly acEreesed the. meeting

The CHAIRMAN said that he had a good deal of sym- pathy with Methedisto and some years aee, he had come across some remarkable utterances of the founder of Methodism in regard to the temperance question. It was those remarks which made him think more and react more of Wesleyan Methodism than he had ever. done before. He foiled that the spirit which animated John Wesley when he spoke perhaps stronger things in. regard to the drink than any living man ever spoke— (applause)—animated the followers of Wesley. He was glad to notice that in connection with the Synod, they put on public record their expression of approval of the attempt which the Government were making to place - the control of that terrible menopoly into the hands of the peeple who had suffered by its being inflicted upen them. I (Applause.) That was one reason why he had a good deal of sympathy with Wesleyan Methodism. Then to ceme Ito local circumstances, he felt a strong sympathy for Sankey Bridges for more reasons than one. He had a, ' ereat many personal friends in Sankey Bridges. He saw one of his oldest friends there—Captain Summerfield. (Applause.) Two of his eons were fellow school metes of his. He had also a good many political friends at Sankey Bridges. They had on occasions rallied to his support, not upon political grounds, but upon grounds that they believed had for their object the better govern- ment, socially and in other ways, of the town in which , they lived. (Applause.) He told them honestly that he did not care to be supported solely upon political grounds. He was determined to do what he could for the town in which he lived to improve the condition of the people, and to make it easier to do right and more difficult to do wrong. His last reason for being there that night was to hear the lecturer. He had heard a great deal about him as au old Warringtonlan. Ho did not know anybody who was in a better position to tell them ' something about the subject of the lecture. He would ask him at once to proceed with the lecture. (Applause.) The Rev. J. G BENNETT said that be was glad to see, Councillor Roberts there that night. He had followed his career in the Council with very much interest, and he had been delighted time after time with the noble stand he had taken on the temperance question. (Ap- plause.) All who had the real good of the people at heart ought to be proud of him. He (the speaker) dis- claimed any idea of his remarks that night being a lecture, but said that it was simply on account of his. work amongst the people as a connexional evangelist of the Wesleyan body.Fle was going to tell them something about this important work. He was going to tell them of some wonderful victories which were won in the name of Jesus Christ. He spent three happy years ha Didsbury College. During the last year, Mr. Clapham,the I Home Missionary secretary, came to him and asked him 'to leave himself entirely in his hands, and not to make any engagement or premise for the coming eenferense of ! 1893. He had a pressing invitation from the Manchester Mission to go there; but he replied "No, I will leave myself in the hands of Mr. Clapham." He came cut of college in July 1893.aiad when he read in the' ManchrsteS Times " that he had been appointed to take up the work of the Rev. Thomas Cook, the connexional evangelist, he would never forget the feeling of his own unworthiness .of the work to which he wa called. After the 1893 conference, he took up his work and since September 1893, be bad travelled between 13,000 and 14,000 miles, north, south, east and west of the British Isles. He had taken 835 services in 528 days. or 107 more than one a day. Be had written over 3,00 J : letters, and he had had the unspeakable joy of leading ' over 4,000 inquirers to Jesus Christ. There were 34 dis- tricts in Methodism, and there were three connexionat evangelists besides Mr. Cook who was in New Zealand. Each district had the right to have one mission by one of the evangelists every yeer, and at the September Synod, it was decided ail which circuit the mission was to be held, and after that the dates for the ensuing year were fixed. His first mission was in September 1893,1 a Denby Dale, three miles from Penistone in Yolkshire. This was a manufacturing village and the people were of a rough class. After some preliminary difficulties, be had I a very successful mission, and had a large ntimber of converts. Mr. Bennett then described in detail his missions in various parts' of the country, and the story was of thrilling interest. Leaving Denby Dale, he went to Uttoreter, thence to Davy Ruling, and on to Beeston Hill (Leeds), Salisbury, Cornwell, Tunbridge Wells,. Huntingdon, C echester. Skinton, North Allertone Richmond, Hastines, Poole, Dorchester, Newtown,. Manchester (Grosven(r-street), Sheffield, St... Ives (Cornwsll). Hu .dersfield, Shetland Isles Falkirk, Tavistoek aril Newton Abbott. The lecturer's account of his visit to the Shetland Isles was very racy and inter- ing, and this portion was without doubt the most inter- estesting part of his lecture.Talting a general survey over Methodism, he said that he was sorry to thdik that the love af the class meeting and the prayer meeting seemed to be dying out in many places. Mere might be greater breadth in Methodism, but it would he a gad thing if that were taken at the expense of depth. He had given the lecture to show them what kind of work the connexional evangelists had to do, and he hoped to have the sympathies and prayers of all the. people. Councillor Roesars expressed the pleasure which he had experienced in listening to the lectute, but said that he did not exactly agree with Mr. Bennett'; somewhat pessimistic views with regard to religeoua influence. He said that municipilities and governments dared not act as thee dared twenty or thirty years ago. A hearty vote or thanks was accorded to the chairman and lecturer on the motion of Mr. James Evans,seconded by Mr. G. Savage. mei supported by the Rev. Jailunnele anti the meeting then terminated.

SATURDAY, MAY 25ra, Mg.

IT is said Lord SALISBURY Lord Salisbury'sbe Latest Speech, dabbler in science, but it must ' allowed by his lordship's blindest - adherent that he completely leaves all scientific methods and reasoning behind him when lie • mounts the political platform. The latest and one' , of the most glaring exhibitions of the defects cl his platform style was given at a Primrose Lege° demonstration on Wednesday. What, for instan°e'. is to be said of the description of the Liberfd majority in the House of Commons as a Enotlef horde" and as" squabbling mercenaries ? " guage of this sort is just a shade too hig"in''' coloured even for a reckless politician of t"es Salisbury type. For, after all, each member the " motley horde " is the ejected. and trusted representative of some consfi' tuency, and therefore fully entitled to sit" in that legislative chamber which all the ablest el' the young peers prefer to the House of Lords. Then how unscientific is the reasoning which Lor- a SALISBURY brings to bear on political In a division at the beginning of the week °n Welsh Disestablishment Bill theGoveroment out with the comparatively small majority of 0.-0 or ten, and, argues Lord SALISBURY, this majority‘ should only count as five because there were foist Unionist seats vacant at the time. gnostic: But weir this is a very lop-sided argument. There Touet-' have been some reason against which Lord SAL-15- BURY shuts his eyes to account for the fact t13,,,t the Government's majority temporarily sank so °J.- as nine or ten, for we Suppose he will admit tbe:',„ that is not the normal majority. Some Libersi- members may have been caught napping for the moment,or it may he, as is now alleged in two -' three cases, some of the Tories may have roteu,,"; against the Government in spite of the fact thso they had paired with Liberals, and were, therefore, bound in honour not to take part in any clivlejoll,,.' These are consi•lerations which the Tory Wee; entirely ignores although they may account for * the smallness of that majority which he wishes ipf' make smaller still. Again, on the subject °- Welsh disestablishment how flimsy are thc, °St" ments of this " scientific " politiciam. On onef hand he practically contends that the 1:1°1 Commons is not entitled to disestablish the IT e f Church because the majority in favour e such a policy would be drawn horn other parts of the United Kingdom—from South-west of Ireland, for instance the other hand he declaims against separate parts, of the Kingdom being endowed with self-goverlr ment because that would be going back to Heptarchy. Between these two stools not 0019 Welsh disestablishment but every other progree' sive measure may well fall to the ground. But Lord SALISBURY must really be a little more reasonable. the He must sit upon either one seat,or the other ; he cannot be allowed to monopolize both. •Oa difficulty of his position is this, that whicheVer choice he takes the case for Welsh disestablish' ment is complete. If he holds that each division; of the United Kingdom must judge for itself, be gives the Welsh Church away entirely, for the local majority in favour of disestablishment is, simply overwhelming. If, on the other hand, he. maintains that these important legislative Pr°- posals should be decided by the combined repro: sentatives of the people the Disestablishment Blf! will still be endorsed. As a matter of fact Lord-- SALISBURY is to some extent in a dilemma. 015 real object is to use the Tory majority the in , 4 House of Lords to frustrate the efforts of a Liberal majority in the House of Commons. This is.a purpose which cannot with discretion be opeaty avowed, and, therefore, his Lordship is driven the use of arguments the weakness and fallacY of which must, one would think, distress his" scion-. tific " conscience. On the subject of tbes. House of Lords itself, Lord Sia't BURY is particularly diverting and unconvincing; He contends, in effect, that the function of hereditary chamber is to check and control tid: House of Commons by rejecting the measure t.O - which in the opinion of their Lordships 511001 d submitted to the people at a general election' use his own words, it is" a body which exists,: , the purpose of preventing the House of CoinTri„, from committing mischief behind the backs a t"0 people." In taking -imp this line he gather ignore the charge that the House of Ilw,r_o is a check upon the House of Commons only se:nil i'g there is a Liberal majority in that House, Pairc,,,t • as they do all the proposals of a Tory Governort cannot ted _ alt with scarcely a murmur. To this fatal indict_ . of the Lords as an effective check upon hasty _leegPo lation what is his reply? Simply this,that Wfi no , Conservative Government is in Pevit,3r „ler legislation of an injnrions character Is

RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RABIES IN CHESHIRE.
An order for the muzzling of dogs came into force on Wednesday in the Cheshire Police districts of Broxton, Eddisbury, Runcorn, and Wirral. DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORN RESIDENT. .

On Sa-t-ti-rd.:y-r-u(;riiing,at an early hour,Thornas of 4, Stanley-st., Runcorn, died after a somewhat pro- longed illness, at the age of 75 years. He came to town from Wigan,and for some years acted as waterman. For a long period, however, he has lived retired. He was exceedingly well-known throughout the district.

div.head: DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: DRUNKENNESS.

At Runcorn Police CiZii;;;'iii;i:sday morning before Mr. T. Handley and Mr. E. Imison, a boatman named John Hillier was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street, the previous day. As the prisoner had several times previously been convicted a fine of 10s. and ss. Bd. costs was imposed or in default fourteen days imprisonment. ST l'Atm's BIBLE CLASS, RUNCORN.

The weekly meeting of this clas's on Sunday afternoon was presided over by Mr. Kniveton who gave the bible lesson. Solos were sung by Mr. C. Atherton who con- tributed 'The New Kingdom," and Mr. Edward Worrall who gave" The Palms." The organist, Mr. William Cooke performed an organ solo. There was a good attendance. BILLIARD MATCH AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday, the rraerebers ot the Runcorn Liberal Club paid a visit to Birkenhead to play a return match with the Liverpool and district team. It will be within the recollection of some that when the Liverpool team visited Runcorn a short :time ago they ran out rather easy victors by 111 points. This they managed to in- crease when the return engagement took place on Wed- nesday. the Liverpool team winning by no fewer than 475 points.

div.head: RUNCORN CYCLE CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN CYCLE CLUB.

Fourteen members of this club participated in the annual inter-club run with the Wigan C.C. on Wednes- day. The place- ot destination was High Legh which was safely reached after a most pleasant ride. Tea was provided at a farmhouse, after which a cricket match was engaged in. The result was a victory for the Run- corn club, who scored 94 runs to their opponents 62.

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE, RITNOO.IIN..
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE, RITNOO.IIN..

Mr. Daniel Iltsbrown presided at the -meeting of this order on Saturday evening. A temperance testimony meeting was held, and the speakers bore eloquent testi- mony to the many and varied benefits they had derived from teetotalistn. The importance of consistent conduct on the part of temperance men was pointed out. The following took part in the meeting :—Messrs. Edward Key, George E. Sutton, William Edgeley, Thomas J. Bolt, Themas Clarke, David Smith, Thomas Whyte, G. Holt, and T. Cooke._ A pleasant evening was spent.

div.head: RUNCORN CONSTABULARY _INSPECTION
div.p: RUNCORN CONSTABULARY _INSPECTION

Sir Herbert Croft, Bart., her Majesty's Government Inspector of Constabulary, accompanied by Colonel Hamersley, chief constable of Cheshire, on Wednesday, inspected the Runcorn division constabulary at their headquart, re, Runcorn. There were on parade Super- intendent Atherton, Inspector Hicks, five sergeants and 25 constables, the other members of the force being on duty. The men were put through military evolutions by Inspector Hicks. Subsequently they were inspected by the inspector who seemed highly pleasei with their smart appearance, and stated that he was well satisfied with the exemplary conduct of the men which was shown by no one having bPen reported for a breach of duty since April 1894.. He afterwards inspected the Police Station and went through the books. FISNERAL OF MISS ETHEL O'KELL.

The death occurred on Saturday night of Miss Ethel O'Kell who was employed at the branch post (ace at Delph Bridge, Runcorn. She had been ailing for a short time and proceeded to the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool, to undergo an operation. This was performed on Fri- day last, and she died the following day. The deceased, who was sister to Mr.C.'Kell postmaster at Weston Point, was buried in Runcorn Cemetery on Wednesday. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. T. Brackenbury, Wesleyan minister, and Messrs. Berrington, Collins, and Riding were present as representatives of the Wesleyan Sunday School, at Weston Point. In addition to rela- tives, a number of friends were also present. Floral tributes were sent by the family, Messrs. J. and E. Roberts, J. and E. Williams (Liverpool),D. and L. Little- more, J. and J. L Littlemore • Mr. :and !Mrs. R. Moore and Miss Campbell, Mr. and Mrs. Leach, Miss Limb, Mr. and lairs.Jones,and Miss Gladys and Master Harold Bain. THE FERRY.

A conference between representatives of the Widnes Town Council, the Runcorn Town Council, and the offi- cials of the Manelyaster Ship Canal Company took place on Wednesday. The business was with reference to the ferry between Runcorn and Widnes. The Mayor of Widnes,Councill )1. Thomas,Mr.Oppenheim (town clerk), and Mr. Sinclair were present on behalf of the Widnes Council ; Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., E. Imison, J.P., R. 11. Posnett, and Mr. F. A. Lake (law clerk), re- presented Runcorn ; and Mr. Hunter (engineer),and Mr. Kershaw (Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw, and Co.), were present for the Manchester Ship Canal Company. The Ines representatives asked for more convenient means of landing, and the:Runcorn gentlemen showed the advantage of elevations of the approach to the ferry so that persons could not only utilise the small boat but join the passenger steamers plying on the waterway. Attention was also called to the fact of a toll being charged for the use of the boat in crossing the Ship Canal in order to reach the boat provided by the London and North-Western RaikVay Company. Mr. Kershaw stated that he was unaware of the latter fact, and pro- mised that it should he inquired into. He and Mr. Hunter would also report the result of the interview to the directors of the Canal Company. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.

In celebration of Ascension Day a special service was held in the Parish Church on Thursday evening, when a festival of the choirs of the Episcopal churches of the tlwn was held, namely,the Parish Church, St. Michael's, Holy Trinity, Weston, and Weston Point. The various choirs assembled in the National Schools, Church-st., and afterwards walked in processional order to the church. There were about 150 voices. The musical part of the service was a special feature and consisted of the singing of several psalms, and the anthem "Lift up your Heads" from the Messiah. The soloists were Masters Lane and lh'oodw Ard. Mr. James Littler was the conductor and he is to be congratulated upon the efficient way the combined choir performed their dutie3, and which showed that great pains had been taken at the rehearsals. Mr. Johnson presided at the organ. The local clergymen present were :—Rev. Canon Wood (vicar), Revs. Dr. Preston, D. S. Bowen, W. H. Stables, A. J. Jameson, H. B. Firth, and A. Bartram. The Dean of Chester (Dr. Darby) preached a powerful sermon, basing his remarks on the text "Thou has ascended on high; thou hast led captivity captive thou bast re- ceived gifts from men" Psalm 68, 18v. The prayers were intoned by the Rev. Canon Wood, and the lessons were read by the Revs. Dr. Preston, and D. &Bowen. THE PROPOSED CEMETERY FOR WIDNES.

Mr. J. S. Sinclair, borough surveyor of Widnes, has prepared plans for the laying out of a portien of the MOM Brook estate, Farnworth, as a cemetery, and the corporation are applying for saction to borrow the money necessary for this purpose. The Moss Brook I estate, which is situated a little over a mile from the centre of the borough, covers 49 acres, and with the buildings upon it has been purchased by the corpora- tion for £5,000. It is now proposed to lay out 15 acres of this land as a cemetery, and this is estimated to cost about £BOO. The cemetery will be divided into three sections—Church of England, Nonconformist, and Roman Catholic—each of whom will have about 3i acres of burial space, while 41 acres will be taken up with walks, buildings, and shructieries the latter extend- ing in a belt all round the cemetery. There will be three Chapels, ono for each religious section. The Roman Catholic Chapel will be on its own section of the ground, but it is proposed to build the Church of England and Nonconformist Chapel close together, and join them by a tower and belfry. The cost of the chapels is estimated at £3,000.
MILL BROW WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. - THE JUBILSF.

On Sunday the jubilee of this Sunday school was cele- brated,when special sermoas were preached by the Rev. George Wood, of Burton-on-Trent, who was at one time stationed in the Runcorn circuit. There were good con- igregations, that in the evening being very large. In his Kiorning sermon the rev, gentleman alluded to the res• ponsibilitv of the Church in the training of children,and ' in seeing that they were thoroughly educated in Christian principles. His evening discourse was based on the text "Show me Thy glory." He mentioned that the Mill Brow Sunday school was established in 1815 in an upper room known as the Quaker's Chapel. The Friends, however, had not held services therein for some time. Mr.Geurge Middlebrook was the first superinterident,and Mr. George Rutter was the first 'visitor. Of those who took part in the o?enity, of the Sundae school Mr. Rutter was the only surviving one. He said he was pleased to see Mr. Rutter in the congregation. When the school opened there were 16 scholars, hut now there were 295 scholars, with a staff of 30 teachers. The expenditure o: the school during the past year was £3O, and he asked for liberal collections. Special hymns and anthems were sung by the choir and scholars under the leadership of Miss Clara Taylor. Mr. H. Pops presided at the organ, and the collections for the day realised .£23. JUDGE WYNNE FFOULICES AND HIS RECENT BEREAVEMENT.

Mr. Joliffe, the registrar of the Runcorn County Court, has received the following letter from his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes in acknowledgment of the eKpression of sympathy made at the pre7ioUS holding of the Court, in his recent bereavement : " Old Northgate House, Chester, May 21, 1895.— Dear Joliffe, I shall be much obliged to you to con- vey to the solictors practising • in the Court, my grateful thanks for their very kind sympathy with me in my great sorrow. Their kindness helps to alleviate my trial. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 25 1895
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 25 1895
DEATH AND FUNERAL OF AN OLD BRIDGEWATER SERVANT. _ .

The remains of Mr. Thomas Pearson, cf English•row, Runcorn, were interred in the graveyard of the Parish Church, Runcorn,ou Thursday afternoon. The deceased, who was 71 years of age, had been engaged by the Bridgewater Canal Company since boyhood. He was well known and greatly respected by his fellow workmen, arid followed his employment until a few weeks ago. The Rev.E.J.Jameson was the officiating clergyman. Among those who joined the funeral procession were Mrs. Pear- son (widow), Mrs. Stmcock,Messrs. Thomas, James,and Samuel Pearson ; Mr. John Grundy, Liverpool (brother- in-law) ; Messrs. Peter,R., T. W., and Charles Grundy, Dr. McKenzie, Mr. W. R. Wads, Mr.W. Sutton,Captains E. Davies, John Pendlebury, H. Taylor, Joseph oidley, William Gibson, Joseph Houldsworth, James Roscoe,and Daniel Hulse.

A BRIDGEWATER CANAL APPEAL In the Appeal Division, on Tuesday an appeal was heard in the case of Grant. Forbes, and Company v. the Manchester Ship Canal Company. It was an appeal by the defendants who asked for j udgment or a new trial in a case tried before Mr. Justice Lawrance land a special jury at Liverpool in March last, in which the plaintiffs, Liverpool merchants, claimed damages for injuriescaused by the plaintiff's barge while navigating upon the Bridgewater Canal at Moor Bridge. The case for the plaintiff was that the barge came in contact with a stone at the bottom of the canal, and that this caused aihole, which,admitting water, spoiling the cargo. The jury for the plaintiff, and allowed £1,200 damages, and against this the defendant appealed upon the ground that the verdict was against the weight of evidence. After arguments the appeal was dismissed.with costs.

div.head: PRIMITIVE ;METHOiiiaT DEMONSTRA
div.p: PRIMITIVE ;METHOiiiaT DEMONSTRA
TION AT FRODSHAM.

The Primitive Methodists in the Preston Brook circuit held a most successful demonstration at Overton Hills, Frodsham, on Wednesday afterrocm. There was a; large company present, and the flue weather which prevailed added not a little to the success of the demonstration. At !three o'clock a service was held in one of the rooms at Mersey View, and was conducted by the Rev. Danzy Sheen. of Sheffield. Amongst those present were the Revs. T. Bramall, H. R. Didcock, and representatives from Primitive Methodist churches in the Preston Brook circuit which comprises Prestou Brook, Runcorn, Fred- sham, Frodsham Bridge, Kingsley, Crowton, Norley, Clifton, Woodbouses, Kingswood and Halton. The ser- mon was preached by the Rev. Datizy Sheen who based I his remarks on the words "Take heed, therefore,how ye hear," Luke viii., 18. The rev, gentleman delivered an excellent discourse in wkich he dealt with several points in the parable of the sower. A collection was taken at the close in behalf the circuit fund. An adjournment was afterwards made to one of the tea rooms where a good tea was provided by Mrs. Parker Home. A meet- ing was afterwards held when the Rev. Danzv Sheen delivered an admirable lecture on the " Rev. C. H. Ppurgeon, his conversion, career, and coronation." At the outset the rev, gentleman spoke of Mr. Spurgeon's ancestry in the Netherlands, his early life at his grand-1 father's house, and subsequently at home with his parents. He then referred to his conversion which took, place in the Primitive Methodist Chapel at Colchester in I 1850, on which occasion the Rev. R. Eaglen was the preacher. Proceeding the rev, gentleman dealt upon Mr. Spurgeon's experience as usher ; his attachment to the Baptist denomination, and his experiences as a boy preacher. '1 he speaker then alluded to the first. pasto r ate of Mr. Spurgeon at Waterbeach, Cambridgeshire, three years after which he was called to the pastorate of New Park Chapel, London, in. 1852. Having incident- a'ly adverted to the success which had attended Mr- Spurgeon's efforts at that place reference was made to the enlargements which were effected at the chapel. During his work at Surrey Gardens Music Hall, Mr. Spurgeon, the speaker said, attracted on an average 10,000 persons to each service. After three years work there, he accepted the Tabernacle pas- torate, which he held from 1861 until the time of his death. During his mission at London he received 14,000 people into his church, and founded a college,orphanage, and other societies. Mr. Sheen then referred to his in- troduction to Mr. Spurgeon and of his becoming a stu- dent at Mr. Spurgeon's college, the use of which Mr. Spurgeon allowed in gratitude to the Primitive Methodis people, in whose church he was converted.—The rev. • gentleman concluded by detailing the celebrated preacher's work as preacher and author until the time of his death.

div.head: SHIP CANAL. --- CANADIAN CATTLE FOR MANCHESTER.
div.p: SHIP CANAL. --- CANADIAN CATTLE FOR MANCHESTER.

The steamship Cynthiana, 2,923 tons, is now on her way from Montreal with 531 head for cattle bound for Manchester direct, this being the first shipment of live cattle to tnis port. The Cynthiana is due on the 257,h inst. If Manchester lairages and slaughter houses are not sufficiently advanced to receive the beasts the cattle will be landed at Woodside and slaughtered in accord- ance with the regulations, A large steamer for Man- chester will also shortly be due with live cattle, horses, &c.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: THE ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD.

The "Manchester Guardian" of Wednesday publishes the following paragraph:—" On April 15 we published a report which was sent to us for publication from the Ship Canal Company's office relating to the accident in which the steamer Harold was concerned at Latchford on the 10th April. We are informed that the report was in reality confidential, and ought not to have been sent to us for publication. In this report a statement was made severely reflecting on Captain Smith, of the Harold. We published this statement with the rest of the report in good faith on the authotity of the Ship Canal Company, but we had, and could have, tic inde pendent means of knowing whether or not it was well founded. As the Ship Canal Company are not prepared to justify the statement of their official we must assume that it was without foundation, and we can have no hesitation in expressing our sincere regret that we should have been the means of giving currency to the report." As the report referred to was quoted from the "Man- chester Guardian" into these columns we c•ncur with the expression of regret that the report was ever published. • -- • -

div.head: MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND THE CANAL. THE OBLIGATIONS CO WARRINGTON AND RUNCORN.
div.p: MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND THE CANAL. THE OBLIGATIONS CO WARRINGTON AND RUNCORN.

The Manchester City Council had an important dis- cussion on Wednesday on the subject of the Ship Canal. —Mr. J. W. Southern moved the adoption of the report of the special coramittee,the effect of which was that the Corporation should accept one-half the interest due on the loan of £5,000,000 next June, namely, £5E3,250. in lieu of £112,500. Mr. Southern said that it the Cor- poration got nothing more when the Christmas interest was due out of revenue—and the accounts showed they would not—there would remain next February a balance of £5.125 on the profits of the loan. It was quite clear that a rate must be laid next year to nay the demands of the Corporation loan- holders. How much it. would be in the pound it was at present impossible to foresee. It would depend upon the earnings of the canal. The sales of plant and the profit on the Bridgewater Canal would he sufficient to pay the interest on the fist and second debentures on the Ist day of January next. The capa- city and utility of the canal had been demonstrated. There was Cause for anxiety,but not for despair. Until they had secured the cotton, the grain, and the cattle trades it was too early to judge of the probable future of the enterprise. In the first four months of last year the Ship Canal traffic receipts were £26,441 ; in the four months just ended they were £36,196. In the first four months of last year, however, the canal was only par daily open for traffic. The prospects were promising- Not only was the progress of the traffic continuous, but indications were not wanting of new avenues of business. Illegal pollution of the river entailed a cost of £25,000 or £30,000 per annum. This they might hope would eventually he materially reduced. In the course of his remarks Mr. Southern said the number of outstanding obligations of the Canal Company was not large. The really important obligations remaining were those to the Runcorn Com- missioners, the Warrington Corporation and traders,and the Salford Corporation. An amicable arrangement had been made with the Runcorn Commissioners by which they agreed to postpone for 25 years the provision of a graving dock, which would have involved an outlay of £50,000. and would have been of very doubtful advantage either to Runcorn or the Ship Canal. At an expenditure of about £5,000 the company was proceeding to construct wharves for large vessels, which would bring trade to the town and revenue to the Canal. Too much could not ' be said in praise of the fair and reasonable, and at the same time prudent. attitude which had been maintained by the Runcorn Commissioners in these negotiations. With regard to Warrington, the obligations imposed were of a most onerous character, and while the Corporation could not be said to have demanded more than their legal rights, powerful and wealthy interests behind the Cor- poration had compelled their insistence upon those rights. Endeavours to negotiate a modification had proved futile, and the result was that a sum of £95,000 had been expended with little advantage to the town. This sum, expended more wisely, would have brought ocean-going ships to their doors, and have enormously promoted the prosperity and importance of the town. The sum set apart for work at Warrington was nearly ex- hausted. There would certainly be no capital to make the dock there, nor were the directors prepared under any circumstances to ask the ratepayera of Manchester o find it. If the Warrington poople waived their dock now they must do as the Manchester people had done—find the money to complete the work th,nn- selves. Mr. Samson seconded the motion for the adoption of the report. Mr. Vaudrey suggested that the Carporation should go to Parliament next November, instead of the year after, and that permission should be asked to suspend the action of the sinking fund, which would colt the rsterayers 411. in tie ponind on the ra.sa. Ltlttr &saw the r:p.L. uttani.noual). I adopted.

div.head: REVIEW OF THE RUNCORN FOOTBALL SEASON.
div.p: REVIEW OF THE RUNCORN FOOTBALL SEASON.
THE FIRST TEAM.

I During the football season which has just closed the Runcorn Rugby Football Club have well maintained their representation as the " Cheshire champions." Of the 32 matches played, 19 were won, five drawn and eight lost. Eight fixtures were abandoned, by reason of frost and other causes. The total score was 15 goals 0 tries in favour of Runcorn, against nine goals,twelve tries scored by opponents, or 189 points against 76. The scorers were :—J. Faulkner,nine tries ; S. Abram,seven; T. Richardson, six ; T. Warder, five ; W. Gayter,three ; S. Walker. three; J. Butterworth, three; 0. Danbavin. two; H. Myers, two; G. Robinson' A. Taylor,J.D vies J. Pendlebury, C. Pendlebury, S. Johnson, F. Barber W. Gregory,W. Faulkner,H. Farmer, one each. Droppe goals were kicked by J. Butterworth, two ; W. Faul ner, one. S. Houghton kicked a penalty goal, and F Cooper scored a goal from a mark. The matches won were Swinton, 2 ; Sale, 2; Birkenhead Park, 2 ; New Brighton, 2 ; St. Helens, 2 ; and Oldham, Salford, Brad- ford. Warrington, St. Helens Recs., Hunslet, Halifax, Widnes, Liverpool Old Boys, and Burton. The matches drawn were with Bradford, Stockport, Halifax, Liver- pool, and Warrington. The games lost were with Widnes, Oldham, Hunslet, St. Helens Recs., Birkenhead, Wigan, Halifax, and Broughton Rangers. The team was again well represented in the Cheshire county matches, though on several occasions the men chosen were unable to take part in the games. The follov ing players were the recipients of county honours : -S. Houghton, T. Warder, S. Abrams, J. W. Faulkner, A. Taylor.J. Langley, F.Gayter, J. Butterworth, J. Davies and J. Stubbs. The matches played by the county team ended in a lose in each instance, although the team played a sound game. They were, however, unfortunate in the results. For the forthcoming season a strong list has been arranged. Tvldesley and Widnes play the two first games at Runcorn, followed by Burton, St. Helens Recreation. Liverpool, Salford, Wigan, St. Helens, Liverpool Old Boys, Bradford, Oldham, Halifax, New Brighton, Manchester, and Stockport. Saturday dates with Warrington are in course of arrangemeut. With this formidable list of matches the team will need to get into early training to start off the team successfully. THE "A " TEAM.

With regard to the " A" team, it mly be stated that although the scoring has hardly been so prolific as last season, yet the fact must not be overlooked that ten matches less have been played than last year. The re- cord is remarkable when the severity of the past winter and the heavy demands made upon them to fill up the Ist team vacancies during the county contests,are taken into consideration. There is one regrettable incident which took place on December 26th, when St. Anne's Parish Church defeated them by a try to nil, this being the only defeat of the season. Over-confidence on this occasion is attributed as the cause of the defeat. Per- haps the best victory achieved was that over Widnes "A " at Widnes, on Easter Monday,when the Runcorn- lens inflicted a crushing defeat. Additional interest was taken in the match inasmuch as each team had only lost one match, and further that'the Widnesians had made a draw at Runcorn in the early part of the season. The Liverpool Rugby Junior League was again joined, but nwing.to the frost five games had to be cancelled, and as the engagements could not be afterwards fulfilled, the team had to abandon the league. There were 24 matches played, of which 22 were won, 1 lost, and 1 drawn, whilst ten games were abandoned through frost. 38 goals and 58 tries were scored against one dropped goal and four tries making a total of 363 points against 16. On four occa- sions only, were the Runcorn lines crossed, which speaks volumes for the defence, whilst the attack has demon- strated itself. Ten matches were played less than Nat season when the record was 34 ma.tchrs played, 30 of which were won and four drawn, scoring 42 goals and 82 tries, against 3 goal.. and 10 tries. The scorers during the season were :—H. Myers, 15 tries; B. West, 10 ; W. Pendlehurv, 9; W. Gregory; T. Richardson. 6; A. C arke : 0. Thinhavin, 5; J. Nickgrm. 4 ; (1. Shaw, 4; J. Light- foot, 3 ; T. div.head: RUNCOTtN CONGREGATIONALISTS AND THE ARMENIAN ATROCITIES.
div.p: RUNCOTtN CONGREGATIONALISTS AND THE ARMENIAN ATROCITIES.
SERMON BY THE REV. J. SIMPSON.

At Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn, on Sun- day evening, the pastor, Rev. John Simpson, preached to a large congregation upon the Armenian atrocities. Re said an outrage had been committed not only against Christianity,but against humanity,and an outrage against humanity ought to be felt by every man. All the world had heard by this time the frightful stery of the oppres- sion, cruelty, and lust in the Turkish Empire. Accounts had come which showed that there could be no longer any doubt that this latest example ef Ottoman misrule and persecution was frightful beyond description, and that which they had heard of lately was only the climax of a long period of cruel tyranny and robbery, ferocity and brutality in which many innocent peonle had lost their lives, their property or their honour. Great Britain was especially resnonsible for the good behaviour of the Turlt,ane. by the Treaty of Rerlin,the Sultan had pledged himself to just and beneficent government of the Christian population. How these solemn obligati:mg had been ignored was notorious—the hills and valleys of Armenia had run with the blood of innocents ; her brave sons and daughters foully butchered ; little babies put to the most painful death. England was not wont to listen with indifference to the imploring appeals of outraged humanity. She had always been looked upon as the champion of the oppressed. Was she now going to lose her grand noble name? Cardinal Manning once said— Oliver Cromwell is not dead, he is only asleep." Would to God he would wake up and get to work in his old fashion on behalf of oppressed Armenia. Not more ' sacred were the hills and valleys of Judea than the blood-saturated hills and valleys of Armenia. Let them ask themselves what was the crime of the Armenians. ' Only that they believed in the gospel of peace and love of Jesus Christ; that they treasured beyond compare tha Bible: that they had in the home one wife and mother rather than a crowd of women robbed of their choicest heritage. The preacher gave a few sickening details of the Armenian atrocities which deeply moved the con- gregation. England as a nation had the unquestioned right to take this matter in hand, and she ought to step in and say, "Such things shall stop at once and for ever." The Armenians ought to have their just and reasonable liberty and protection. They ought further to insist upcn the villains being brought to justice, not I merely because the Armenians were Christians, hut be.- cause they were men and women whom they had pledged to shield and protect. !hymn jiNtiCe was tardy and might be delayed by diplomatic dilly-dallying, though the Euronesn Powers were moving at last. Let the voice of England say, " There has been enough delay, and Armenia mo4t have justice. At the close of the address there was a very impres- sive scene The preacher said that he wanted them to do something nractinal in the matter. Would those who were in favour of petitioning the Government rise ? The whole congregation rose err moose. The f olowinT was the petition read by the pre.cher.:—" That this con.rogation, deeply moved and horrified by a rerif.sl of the cruelties perpetrated upon the Armenian Christians, the accounts of which had been fully confirmed by the commission of inquiry appoint,:d by Russia, France, and Great Britain, entreats her Majesty's Govern --ent not to relax its rfforts in the cause of our common humanity I until such reforois have been instituted in the govern- ment of Armenia, under the supervision .and with the annroval nf the above-named European Powers, as will off eetuallr nrevent A repetition of such abominable crimes iu the future."—The Ray: J.SiaapsJtj promised to at once forward the above petition to Lord Kimberley, the Foreign Secretary.

div.head: I NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETIC.
div.p: I NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETIC.
CRICKET.

Warrington were unable to maintain the brilliant form which they showed against Manchester, when they opposed the Broughton team on Saturday. R. Smith was the only player who could do anything against the bowling of Sharpe and Braddock, and his score was 25. Mr. "Extras" was the next highest scorer with 10, no that it will be seen that the other members of the team made very little between them, and the total score was Four " ducks " were obtained, viz., by Callon,llind, diaiore and Bibby.

The Broughton mien very easily passed the Warrington Dtal, although their innings was marred by a reffretable acident. At the commencement of J. A. Darbyshire's . finings he was caught by Clark, at least everybody but the umpire said so, and as this gentlemen gave him not out to his own and everyone else's surprise, he was al- lowed to proceed, and as is often the case on similar occasions when a man has had a narrow escape,he played so carefully that all the efforts of the Warrington bowlers and fielders failed to get him out, and be carried his bat out for 74, thus alone passing the Warrington total by twelve. Warrington 'Were thus extremely unfortunate, as but for this occurrence, the Broughton victory would have been much less prominent than three wickets and 79 runs.

E. Connor maintained his reputation as a bowler, and he appears to have almost as much control over the cricket ball as over the Association football. His analysis was four wickets for 34 runs. Bates obtained two for 31. Smith was expensive as he only obtained ene for 37, but he was most difficult to play as was shown by the fact that out of 22 overs, there were 13 maidens. Three other Warrington bowlers were tried but they failed to get a single wicket.

R. Smith is now in undisputed possession of the top position in average, and will proNbly keep there for some considerable time at least. He has now completed his hundred runs. The following is the averaoe of those who have played three innings with an average of over three : Times
Inns. not out. Runs. Average. R. Smith J. Calton G. Clarke 766 W. Wordsworth. 4 ... 0 ... 28 ... 7•00 Clark (A) ... 1 ... 19 ... 633 Bates 625 J. Bibby

The second team were much more fortunate than their seniors, and Broughton had a very lively time of it indeed. Hampson defied all their bowlers and was not out for 58, while Crompton obliged with 50, Duckworth with 32. Rushworth with 23, and Silcock with 17 not out. So prolific was the scoring that the Warrington innings were closed with only seven wickets down for I the formidable score of 206. Broughton could only reply with 145, and thus h id as good a beating as Warrington first received at Broughton.

The Sankey Wesleyans owed their victory over C.L.C. Engineers to the middlernen,and to good bowling,. They started none too well, the first six batsmen doing very little, but Light with 10 not out, Bennett 12. and Booth 18, put a different complexion upon the f".• mo. and the score of 65 was the result. Harrison wa ch.. most des- tructive C.L.C. bowler. The Engii.e 'old not do anything against the excellent bov"iii! .4 Beaman, Bailey, and Watkins, and were all out for 29, Watkins in particular was in excep t,,rm with the ball, for he to)k four wickets at UAL: atoll cost of three runs.

The Periketh Wesleyans did not come up to their form of the previous week, and they suffered defeat from Y.M.C.A. by 85 to 31. They would do better if their fielding were a little better. By the way, Mr. Sanders, the secretary of the Y.M.C.A.cricket club,would be glad to open up a. correspondence with secretaries of other clubs with a view to forming a junior cricket league for next season. A junior cricket league is very desirable, as it seems a pity that with so many junior teams in existence the matches are only desultory ones, so to speak ; and that there is no system at present for proving which is the best club in the district. Mr. Sander's suggestion is a good one, .nd deserves to be taken up.

The Cairo-st. Unity,both first and second, had a parti- cularly bad time of it on Saturday, for the first only scored five, and the second only seven. Peter Walker and Sons' bowlers had their averages considerably im- proved by these two matches, and the Unity must have felt very small indeed when the games were over.

The first class cricket season is already in full swing. It will be difficult to find any previous season when there were so many centuries and double centuries:scored in so short a time. Such monster scores as we have had are very like the Australian figures, and should the weather continue favourable there ought to be a good number of batsmen who score their thousand runs this season.

Lancashire are commencing well, for following their ten wickets viltory over N.C.C. they beat Sussex this week by seven wickets. This is a new experience to the Lancashire supporters, for generally the team has com- menced in a most disastrous fashion, and then towards the close they have carried all before them. They have lost the championship several times in this manner. They have tv.gun woll this year and it is to be hoped that they will end as well.

A very satisfactory feature of the Lancas'aire team ts that they appear to have lost their "tail." It has been usual in previous seasons for the first two or three bats- men to malo good scores and then for the remainder to do practically nothing. The present team appears to be a much more even one, and the last corners are to be reckoned with as well as the Brat. Oalv one player,Paul, has won the unwelcome pair of Fn.ctacles so.far,but he atoned for this by his smart fielding.

Sussex. are doing badly, and have lost all their matches tin to date, which is, however, not an unusual thing with them. It is rather surprisine• to find Notts, who last week broke the record of county cricket, by scoring over 700 against Sussex, dismissed twica this week by Leic.stershire. one of the " second class" counties of last year. for totals of 91 and 1.20. This either shows well for Leicester howling or does not say much for the Sussex bowling. Leicester are com- mencing sensationally, and for the time being head the championship list of the counties, having beaten both Notts and Surrey. It is evident that they will have to be reckoned with.

Warwickshire who commenced so well last year are doing the reverse this year. They have already played four matches, and two with Derbyshire and Essex were drawn, and two with Surrey and Yorkshire were lost. They were. however, extremely unfortunate with York- shire, for 100 rune had to be scored in 60 minutes by Yorkthire to win the match, and yet this feat was ac- complished, Brown the hero of the Australian tour being in a great measure responsible for it. Gloucestershire have actually begun this season with a win, which is a rather astonishing feat, as they are usually at the bot- tom or thereabouts of the championship table. W. G. Grace, however, was in his merriest mood, and 288 is something for the Somerset bowlers to study.

It is rather surprising that notwithstandino. the heavy scoring of the present season, none of the members of the AustrAlian team have done anything phenomsnal. They are perhaps "biding their time," and will no doubt surprise the natives some fine afternoon. None of them have, at any rate, scored a hundred yet.

div.head: SWIMMING.
div.p: SWIMMING.

The expected season of -activity was fairly launched by the first gala at the Baths on Tuesday evening when all the arrangements !lel • a night of pleasure and excitement. In the hanclic4p4,comprising 18 heats, almost all the comoetitors turned out and some valiant struggles for supremacy were witnessed. Tyers,too,waS as popular as ever, and -.vhen he succeeded in lowering his own record for 100 yards, even though by only the fraction of a second, the sp.ctators were not slow in according him the praise which W-1.1 his due, and which was further extended to hint for his wonderful feat of winninff the final in the handicap after being " scratched "at 23 seconds. The boy members of the well-known Osborne-street Swimming Club proved themselves to be efficient life-savers, and the precramme of the evening was one which on the whole did credit to its organisers.

Naturally a large fund of enthusiasm was reserved for the all•important polo match, initiating the Liverpool and District League competition. Since last season when the results were .so satisfactory the Warrington team has undergone some notable and apparentiv valu- able changes. Locker is captain :pica Turner, who now does yeoman service as right forward. W. Ashton plays as left forward, while Scotson is berthed in the situation most suited to his powerful throw, that of half back. The working of this combination was highly satisfactory though it would be a decioed advantage if &ghton could become possessed of a portion of Bearnan's weight and the latter some of Ashton's speed.

In the match itself the first thing to become promin- ent—disagreeably prominent—was the unusual number of fouls which the referee was constrained to call. To the credit of the Warrington teatn it may be said that their mis behaviour in this respect was as nothing com- pared with that of the visitors whose endeavour it seemed to be to "down" on opponent when he looked dangerous. This is mistaken policy, as in quite half the instances Warrington were greatly benefirted hy the respite and relief which this cessation of play afforded. Notwithstanding, Warrington had decidedly the best of matters and from first to last the North Liverpool Gym- nasium team had hardly a look in, though the score only brnounted to four goals against their nil,

div.p: Locker was never more prominent than on Tuesday night when without a single exception on the throwing out of the ball, after a restart, by the referee he was first to secure and thus put his side immediately on the offen- sive. The plan is for the captain on capturing the leather, to pass to the best placed man, who, if the way is clear, puts in a rapid shot at goal with every probabil- ity of taking the goal-keeper off his guard. This desideratum gained,Locker pushes forward to the visitor's goal where he remains on the look-out for the passes and stray-shots which continually fly that way. Twice from this position Locker scored and also placed a third goal to his credit from the side. Though such good work was being done at the front, all the skill was not centred there, for Turner, Scotson and Furness, made repeated efforts to score, but were always frustrated. Their efficiency was not to be doubted, however.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR. -FRANK SPEAKMAN,
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. -FRANK SPEAKMAN,
OF RUNCORN.

At St. Helen's Church, Witton, Northwich, the marri- age of Mr. Frank Speakman, son of Mr. and Mrs. J. J. Speakman, of Runcorn, with Miss Edith Jane, daughter ot Mr. and Mrs. H. E. Woodward, of the "Crescent," Northwich, was solemnised by the Rev. W. H. 13inney, M.A., vicar on Wednesday. The bride was attired in a dress of cream corduroy, trimmed with China silk, and wore a tulle veil with a wreath of real orange blossoms. She carried a bouquet of white blooms, the gift of the bridegroom. In attendance upon her were four brides- maids, viz. : Miss Eva Woodward (sister of the bride), Miss Walton, and Misses Eva and Gladys Speakman' sisters of the bridegroom Miss Eva Woodward wore a dress of white delaine, trimmed with primrose silk, and Miss Walton wore a dress of primrose nun's veiling, trimmed with China silk, and both had large picture hats, trimmed with primrose sbot ribbon. The Misses Speakman wore frocks of cream s. trimmed with buttercup silk, and large leghorn its trimmed with buttercup silk and white ostrich tips. 'Fhe bridesmaids carried bouquets of marguerite dais( s and ferns, while the mothers of the bride and bridegroom carried posies of beautiful flowers. The bridesmaids also wore adornments of gold rings and brooches, the gifts of the bridesgroom. Mr. W. H. . Savage, of Runcorn, officiated as best man, and the other groomsmen were Messrs. G. H. Woodward, Eric Speakman, and Albert Jacobs. The bride was given away by her father. The friends , assembled were Mr. and Mrs. Woodward, Mr. and Mrs. IJ. J. Speakman, Mr. and Mrs. Burgess, Master Harold Burgess, Mr. and Mrs. Cowley, Miss Walton, of Halton ; Miss Roberts, of Liverpool ; Mr. Davies, Mr. J. Sherratt, Miss Jacob, and Mr. A. Jacob. After tho ceremony, luncheon was partaken of at the residence of the bride's parents. During the afternoon, Mr. and Mrs. Frank Speakman departed for Windermere, where they intend to spend the honeymoon. div.head: MURDER OF X STOCKPORT ALDERMAN.
div.p: MURDER OF X STOCKPORT ALDERMAN.
SUICIDE OF THE MURDERER.

A murder of a sensational and peculiarly determined character was perpetrated at Stockport on Thursday. The victim was Mr. John Marshall, an alderman of the borough ; and the murderer, who atterwards committed suicide, was a man named James Barrow. The crime appears to have been carried out with relentless delibera- tion. There is a suggestion, of which more, perhaps will be heard, that Barrow's action was inspired by a powerful motive ; but whatever that motive may have been—whether it was one of revenge or not,—it did not hinder the murderer from laying his plans with perfect precision. One on the articles found on his body was a return ticket from London Road Station, showing that he had travelled from Manchester by a train that would ' bring him to Stockport in time to intercept Mr. Marshall on his way to business. The apparently trivial circum- stance that Barrow had obtained a return ticket leaves room for doubt as to whether he may not, after all, have contemplated another termination to the encounter, but the suggestion receives no support from what is known of the actual circumstances attending the crime. The theory, on the contrary, that Barrow had prepared, and , doubly prepared, for the worst seems to be strongly I borne out by the fact that besides reserving two cham- bers of his revolver for contuagencies after the murder, he had also supplied himself with poison. Short as the story of the crime is, the deed itself was accomplished in fewer moments than it will take to read the narra- tion. &fore nine o'clock in the nsorning a, man, then unknown, was seen standing by the gate of Mr. Marshall's building yard, opposite the Star Inn, in Higher Hillgate. The stranger ' was smokinx a cigar, and appeared to be waiting for someone. Mr. Marshall arrived shortly after nine: o'clock, and at twenty minutes past nine an employe in the yard named Patrick Moran obseived the stranger ' enter the office. Thera was nothing remarkable in any of these incidants, and Moran, believing that an ordinary business transaction was in progress,continued to occupy himself with his work. He was suddenly startled by the sound of three shots fired in rapid succession. As he rushed towards the office he heard two more shots fired. Entering tht building, he was arrested on the very threshold by what he saw. His employer had evidently sought to escape from the inner office, but had been caugut in the lobby, and turning to face his antagonist I had been immediately shot. As Moran opened the door Mr. Marshall was in the act of falling, while the other ' man was groping his way backwards towards the dear. The faces of both were stained with blood. On reaching the door Barrow fell, and thereupon Moran sought to enter with the intention of assisting his master. Barrow, who must now have been almost in the agony of death, gave one more example, even at this extremity, of his amazing determination. He turned on his side and levelled the revolver at Morao,who hastily withdrew and ran into the street. Here he met Police Sergeant Taylor who happened to be on duty in the vicinity. The officer returned with Moran to the scene of the crime, and on entering the office found Mr. Marshall lying in the lobby face downwards, but alive and conscious, while the other man, apparently quite dead, lay almost in the position in which-Moran had left him, his right hand still clutch- ing the revolver. Mr. Marshall died a few moments later, without, as far as anyone knows, having uttered a word.

div.head: MILTON CON G REGATIONAL CHURCH,
div.p: MILTON CON G REGATIONAL CHURCH,
WIDNES.

On Thursday evening a special gathering was held in connection with the above church, for the purpose of recognising the Rev. Edward Austin as pastor. Mr. Austin commenced his ministry in Widnes on Easter Sunday, having previously been engaged at Marsh Gibbon, near Bicester, Buckinghamshire. The proceed- ings on Thursday evening took the form of a tea and meeting. Tea was partaken of by about 80 members and friends. The following ladies had charge of the arrangements for tea :—Mesdames Austin, Ainsworth, Way, Hulme, Rogers, Lamb and Misses Thomas, Evans, ,1 and Lamb. The meeting, at which there was la good attendance, commenced about seven o'clo k, under the presidency of Mr. E. Sherrock Eccle.i, of Liverpool. chairman and treasurer of the Liverpool District of the Lancashire Congregational Union, who was supported by the Revs. E. Austin, J. A. Mitchell, B.A. (St. Helens), John Simpson, M.A. (Rue- corn), George Lloyd Stanley (Liverpool), H. F. Spencer, 8.A., M.Sc. (Wavertree), and A. H. Sayers (Frodshare). Among others present were Messrs. E. Lloyd Jones, %V. Handley, and Beck (Runcorn), T. J. Peters, E. Thomas, J. Thomas, W. Streets,and the following church officers: —Mes.rs. Councillor Fiodgkinson, %V. Ainsworth, Joseph Reay, William Horning, J. Hulme, J. S. Rogers, W. Bartrop, and W. J. Baggeridge. After the reading of a portion of scripture by the Rev. H. Sayers, and prayers by Mr. Linyd Jii,nes, the Rev. J. Simpson, on behalf of the mother church at Runcorn, welcomed Mr. Austin to Widnes,and proceeded to speak upon " What his hearers may expect from the preacher." He said they expected him to to, true to his God and to preach the gospel fear- lessly.—The Revs. G. Lord, H. Spencer and others ad- dressed the meeting.

The Marquis of Queensberry and Lord Douglas of Hawick were charged on Wedliesday at Marlborough- Police Court, London, with disorderly conduct in Piccadilly. They were bound over in their recognisances of £5OO each to keep the peace for six months.

A summary of accounts issued under the receiving order made against Henry Granville Wright,lately solici- tor to the Balfour companies, shows gross debts of £16,188, and assets of £10,139. At Bow-street Police Court on Thursday, Jabez Spencer Balfour was formally committed for trial on various cbarges of conspiracy and fraud.

ABRIDGED PROSPECTUS. This Comoany was formed in November, 1894, for the pur- pose of : (1) Constructing and working a tramroad about 42 miles inleo.gth, from Llanberis to a point at the summit of Snowdon. (2) Acquiring a lease of, and carrying on, the well-known Victoria Hotel, Llanbivis, situAed near the commence- ment of the tramroad. (3) Erecting, furnishing, and carrying on the Summit Hotel, at the upper terminus( f the trammed, 3,500 feet above the sea level. The Victoria Hotel has been in the company's possession since November last, and, in the interval, extensive improve- ments have been made, and the sanitary arrangements re- modelled noon the most approved principles. Mr. G. W. D. Assheton-Smith and ths trustees of the will of the late Mrs. Asshetoo-Sinith have conveyed to,ntte com- pany In fee the whole of the land required for thenrammad and stations, and this has b-2eu carried out without Parlia- mentary powers. The Victoria Hotel, with 32 acres of land adjoining, In which is situated the celebrated Dolbadarn Castle, together with the exclusive right of fishing in the Upper Lake, is held by the Company under a lease from Mr. Assheton- Smith for 50 years, front the 12th November, 1894, at the rent of £220 per annum, with the option to the Company to deter- mine the lease at, the expiration of the first five years. The busin'SS of the hotel has been carried on without a break and will be continued on the lines of a first-class modern hotel. A spacious and attractive refreshment room, with recreation grounds adjoining, will be erected at the lower terminus of the tramroad. which it is expected will materi- ally add to the profits of the CO M patsy. The present iss,e of *20,000 D3bentures is made to meet the expenditure upon hotels, lands, and other matters, not Included in the contract for the tramroad works. The £15.0)0 balance will be issued only if and when required. The De- bentures will constitute a first charge as a floating security upon the entire undertakinis And property of the Company. • Shareholders will be preferentially considered in the allot- ment of the Dec entures. The tramroad being the first of its kind in the United Kingdom it may be desicable to compare the estimated traffic with that of a foreign mountain line of similar charac- ter. The one that appears most nearly to resemble the Snowdon Tramway is the Rigi-bahn, or railway up the Rigi mountain, so well known to all travellers in Switzerland. It is found that this line has, during the years 1892, 1893. and 1894, paid a steady dividend of 8 per cent. on a c Apital of £50,000, and that this dividend was paid after paving interest on £38,000 of debentures ; that during the year 1893 they carried 45,177 passengers, and their gross revenue, including some goods and luggage traffic, was 295,576 francs, or £11,823, this without any revenues from hotels. Copies of the memora cttim and articles of associaiion of the same-mentioned doouments, and of the form of Deben- ture, can be si en at the offices of the solicitors of the Com- pany. Applicatiems for Shares and Debentures should be made on tire enclosed forms, accompanied by the payment of 10s. per Share and £lO per cent, on the Debenture, Stock, and should be sent to the bankers, or to the secretary at the offices of the Company.
