div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
AN EX-COMRADES ESCAPADE.-STEALING A PONY AND TRAP.

At the Warrington Boreugh Court on Tuesday, before Mr. R. Garnett and Dr. T. Starkey Smith, John Hunt was charged with stealing on May 17th a pony and trap, knee rug, harness, and whip, valued £6O, the property of Joseph Craik. The Chief Constable said that the com- plainant was a rope and twine manufacturer,whose rope walk was in Battersby-lane,and who resided at Brick-st. His son, Mr. Joseph Craik, jun., who would he the chief witness, resided with his sisters in Arpley-st. 'Me de- fendant was an ex-cenvict, and was well-known to the police at Blackburn, Preston, and Manchester. Mr. Craik, jun., had been to Northwich on Friday. and on coming to Warrington he stopped at the" Blue Bell,"and the prisoner was engaged to take the pony and trap to the stable in Brick-st. It was, however, subsequently discovered that he had never been there, and on Sunday morning information was given to the police. Inspector Spinks recollected that at one o'clock on Saturday a telephonic message had been received from Preston that a pony and trap supposed to have been stolen from War- rington had been seized by the police of that town, but as no information had up to that time been received by the Warrington police, nothing further was done. Upon Mr. Craik making the complaint,the Preston police were telephoned to. and it was discovered hat the pony and trap answered in every respect a) the description given and Mr. Craik, jun., and Detective Monaghan went on Sunday afternoon to Preston, and the pony and trap were identified. The prisoner was brought before the Preston magistrates on Monday morning, and was then given in charge of I:tective Monag- han, who brought him to Warrington. Joseph Craik, jun., gave corroborative evidence, stating that when he stopped at the Bluebell Inn he asked Mr. Kershaw. the landlord, to find a man to take the pony and trap to the stable in Brick-street.—William Kershaw said he assisted his mother to keep the " Bluebell," said that he thought that the prisoner was a Warrington man, otherwise he waiild not have allavred him to take the pony and trap.—James Cuerden, horse slaughterer, 3 Mount Pleasant, Preston, said that on Saturday morn- ing at alma ten o'cleck prisor.er came with the pony to his place of business. The pony appeared to he dis- tressed as though it had come a long way. The prisoner , asked witness whether he would buy it and asked £9 I for it saying it was his own. He represented himself as " tatter,"and said he had come from Holmes Mill. Witness examined the pony, and found it was worth more than £9. Prisoner put the pony in a gig to try it, and witness in the meantitne informed the police, and prisoner was arrested.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said that he received the prisoner in custody from the, Preston police the previous day. He brought him to ! Warrington and charged him with the theft, and he re. ! plied, " A man asked me to mind the horse, and I drove it to Preston. I tried to sell it. I told the police where the trap and harness was."—Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.—The beach ex- pressed their appreciation of the manner in which the witness Cuerden had acted, and said that as he was thei chief means of recovering the pony and trap, they hoped that Mr. Craik would suit ably acknowledge him. TROUBLESOME CHARACTERS SENT TO GAOL.

Two well-known characters, Peter Higgins and Annie Ryan, were brought before the Warrington magistrates on Tuesday, charged with stealing from John Mitchell, in the Star and Garter public-house on Monday, a purse containing £2. The Chief Constable stated that the complainant was a farm labourer at Pemberton Farm, near St. Helens, Higgins, the male prisoner, was a street loner, and Wai never known to wok, while Annie Ryan was also well-known in tha% court. Mitchell cams to Warrington on Monday morning about ten o'clock and had a purse in his possession, containing £3. He called at one or two public-houses with some friends, and as about ten minutes past seven, at night, he wept ino-o the Star and Garter, Friars' Green,where he paid for a clam t of beer. The two prisoners came in at this time, and they had a drink of this glut of Wee. Aaother quart was also pal I for, after which. Biggins commenced a single step dance. He then invited Mitchell to dance with him, and he put his arin round him, and was seen to put his hand in Mitchell's pocket, and take the puree out. He was also seen to hand the purse end its con- tents to Annie Ryan. The complainant hereupon cried out that he was robbed. The landlord in a roost praise- worthy manner shut all the doors of the house, and sent his wife for the police. Before the police had arrived, however, the two prisoners had escaned, and upon searching the house, the complainant's purse, emptied of its contents was found in the Pre-place. The prisoners were arrested the same night. The complaineet was , perfectly sober at the time of the theft. Evidence 'corroborating Mr. Hunt's statement was given by Detective-Sergeant Monaghan, John Hansbery, Thomas Mullins (the landlord of the Star and Garter), Hannah Healey, and Elia theth Mullins. The magistrates decided to send each prisoner to gaol for three mouths. Annie Ryan, upon hearing the sentence, became very abusive, and as P.C. Turner was taking her out of the Icourt-room, she raised her hand when passing the wit- Incas, Healey.. and a sound similar to that caused by a ' blow in the face was heard. This was accompanied: by the most violent language, and she asked the bencn to "put it on while they were at it." She was then brought hack, and charged with assaulting the Witnes‘ Hannah Healey in the court, but she denied this, and P.C. Turner and Healey also said that no blew had been struck. The Chief Constable, and many others in the court were however of the opinion that she had struck Healey, but the bench gave her the benefit of :he doubt; and did not inflict a heavier penalty. They informed 'tset. that had the assault been proved, they would have dealt severely with her. MERCILIISS , BRUTALITY. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Thursday, before the Mayor (chairman) and Mr. J. H. Fleming, Patrick Edward Macdonald was charged with tieing druuk and disorderly in Dallam-lane at 10 20 on Wed- nesday moraine ; he was further charged with asesult- ing Catherine S.uith at the same time, and also charged with wilfully damaging windows to the value 01 61 ,the property of James Hill.—P.C. Bell said that on the day named he saw the defendant in Back Denim-lane, drunk and using obscene lamluage. He was bleeding from the hands, and on making enquiries witness found that de- fendant had broken nine panes of glass with his fi3t. Mrs. Smith was bleeding from a cut over her right eye and had a swelling over her left temple. He was broualit to the pollee station where his wounds were dressed. Witness then went to Smith's house arid found that de. fondant had struck at her with a kettle, the blow just touching her head and then descending on the table which caused the handle to he bent, showing the free of the blow. He also menaced her with a knife which he stuck in the table.—Elizabeth Ellen Smith, niece of complainant gaee corroborotive evidence, in which she stated that defendant in addition knocked complainant down and kicked her. He also struck witness.— Catherine Smith, who appeared with the top half of her face and both eyes badly blackened, and a strip of plaster over the right temple, said that defendant had struck her with his fists, but denied that he attempted to strike her with either the kettle or the knife. She herself was to blame in the matter.—The Mayor said de- fendant '8 behaviour to the woman was something awful he would not have treated a dog like thar,and defendant would have to go to gaol for two months' with hard lab- our.

div.head: • THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 25, 1895.
div.p: • THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 25, 1895.
PETTY TnErrs.—TWO BEGINNERS OF EVIL.
The magistrates at.. the .Warrington P,•liee Court on

Thursday had before them the case-of Catherine Murray . domestic servant, from St. Helens, who was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of John Stapleton, 11, Geest., on the 7th May, an apron, valued 9d. was also charged with stealing another apron on the 21.4 t May.—Defendant, who seemed very penitent, pleaded guilty to both charges. The Chief Constable stated to the magistrates that defendant had been living at com- plainant's house during the last three weeks. On Tues- day Mrs. Stapleton missed one apron from the clothes line and defendant was also away. Having her suspi- cions the matter was reported to D S. Monaghan, who saw defendant and taxed her with the theft, when she said, "1 don't know whatever came over me to do it." —The magistrates recorded a convictiou, and defendant was then dismissed.

Sarah Warburton, 18, living at Clothhall-yard, was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of Mr. Murphy, 2, Clothhall-yard, a quantity of bacon, value 14. 4d. Mr. Hunt said that on Wednesday morning Mrs. Murphy asked defendant to look after the baby whiie she went out. When she came back she noticed that a piece had been taken from her bacon. Monaghan was communicated with and visited defendant, who said, " Yrs, I took it ; I cut it myself." As this was her first offence she was dismissed with a conviction recorded against her.

EARLESTOWN V. LIVERPOOL.—A team, which included three professionals, Goodwin, Sharpe and Ringrose, representing Liverpool visited the Earlestown ground on Saturday to play the first of the home and home fixtures. The eleven was considered to be a fairly strong one, and numbered the two Mellys' two Harrisons,and Wakefield. The heme captain won the toss, and elected to go to the wickets first, Husband and Dennis facing the attack of Goodwin and Ringrose. Careful play became the order, the batsmen at once discovering that the bowling was rot to be treated lightly. Dennis opened the norms; by lilting Ringrose for a single,which Husband followed up by sending Goodwin to the boundary. Dennis after another single gave Goodwin a hard chance, but he failed to hold it, and Husband brought him round to thei boundary. The next ball Dennis sent back into Good- win's hands. Miller joined Husband, and after several futile attempts he brought Goodwin round to thel boundary, and after twice repeating the feat, he was bowled by Goodwin, his contribution being 11. Nokes filled the vacancy, but the partnership was of short duration, Husband being c and b by Ringrose. Bell joined Nokes, but he unfortunately skied the second ball he received, which H. C. Harrison held. Crowther, a promising young bat, partnered Nokes,ani after negoti- ating Ringrose, Nokes lifted Goodwin to the boundary, and smirked him for the sane number. Crowther re- peated the dose. After some desultory play in which Crowther showed excellent style, Nokes again secured a boundary and Crowther followed suit off Ringrose. With 50 up, A. L. Melly replaced Goodwin at the bottom wicket, the change having the effect of removing Nokes, who was smartly taken at point by A. J. Melly, his con- tribution being 20. Clare joined Crowther, and drove his first ball to the boundary, but was shortly after caught behind the wicket by Wakefield. Alderson filled the vacancy, but scoring was remarkably slow, singles coming at rare intervals. Alderson finally got hold,and drove Melly for a couple, and after one or two maiden overs, he played on to his wicket. Barker replaced him, and the score increased a little more rapidly, although Crowther continued to play careful but correct cricket. Barker after contributing 5 was stumped, and Mitchell took his place. After a creditable inuings f.,1 21, Crowther was caught by Ringrose off Melly. Emmett filled the last post and at once commenced to hit out, bringing about another bowling change. H.C. Harrison displacing Ringrose, and after a couple of overs Good- will went on vice Melly. Several runs were added by both batsmen, but Mitchell's career was cut short by Harrison, and the winnings ended for 97. For Liverpool A. L. Melly and Sharpe took first place at the wickets, Bell and Clare bowling. Bell opened the attack, and off the third ball, Sharpe was cleverly taken by Husband. Rowley replaced Sharpe, but with the score at 19, Melly was cleared bowled by Bell. A procession afterwards followed,Ball being in grand form, while Clare from the bottom end secured two of the wickets, until the advent of B. C. Harrison, who with Rusvley hit out freely and the score mounted rapidly. At 50 Husband went on vice Clare, Rowley,after adding 27, being neatly bowled by Bell. Ringrose joined Har- rison, hut he was sent to the right about with the first hall. Wakefield fared little better and after contributing 3,he was bowled by flusband.Goodwin filled the vacancy but after adding a single he was caught by Alderson,the innings closing for 76. The fielding 3f the Liverpool men was a treat, and also was the bowling of Bell, and the victory gained by Earlestown was meritorious. Scores: EARLESTOWN. LIVERPOOL.

RUNCORN v. WIDNES.—Played on the Widnes ground, on Saturday, before a small attendance. The turf was in excellent condition. Going in first Runcorn knocked up the highly respectable total of 81. Gone was dis- missed before the double figures had been attained, but Wright and Abrams carried the score to 20, when the latter was dismissed by a tine catch by Williams. Jea- cock and Arinsworth got together and punished the bowling somewhat unmercifully,the;former driving Reay to the on for a couple. The home fielding was some- what loose, and to this must be added a large number of the visitors' runs. Cragg and Abrams took up the at- tack for Runcorn, but a vigorous stand was made by Harrison and Smith. Both batsmen displayed sound Judgment, and runs caind freely from the start. Harri- son cnt a single, followed this up with a brilliant drive to the pailings, and Smith was cheered for an effective strike or two. After a productive partnership Smith was dismissed and Hampson filled the vacancy. After mak- ing three he was clean bowled by Abrams, Parkinson, the new comer was instrumental in securing 9 runs,and the score gradually rose. div.head: 'MIN olt CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT.
div.p: 'MIN olt CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT.
FliMAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alder- man T. E. Wiight, and Dr.. Gornall.

A TRIVIAL CHALIGR.—John flenry Birchall,Eustace-st., was charged with having on the 14th May committed wilful damage to a clothes line, the property of Ann Wynne,Eustace-st.—lt appeared that defendant bad cut complainant's line because she had pushed away a fence of his, arid he was provoked. Defendant promised not to repeat the offence,and to live on friendly terms with complainant, and he was dismissed on paying the costs.

FAMILY Jam William Bibby, Winwick•road, W 45 charged with committing wilful damage to a looking glass, picture, and clock on the 11th May, the property of Elizabeth Shepherd.—Defendant admitted breakinu the picture and looking glass, which he said were his own.—The evidence showed that defendant is the son of complainant, and that there was constant bickering be- tween them. The case was dismissed on payment of costs.—Clara Bibby,wife of last defendant, was charged with using threats to Elizabeth Shepherd, on the 23:h I April. The complainant said that (lefendnnt had used threats to her so that she was afraid she would do her an injury. Ai the case was merely a development of the other, the case was dismissed, and the Chairman said he never saw a more disgraceful row got up between rela- tives in his life than the one then before them.

USING THREATS.—James Manly was charged with having on the 12th May used threats to Mary Ann Green.—Complainant said that on Sunday night the de- fendant came to her door and asked her to turn her hus- band out as he (defendant) would kill him in live minutes. Witness replied, "Jim where's your burying ground as you bury your dean." Hs then threatened her. It was stated that defendant had been assaulted by complainant's husband, and in the end the bench dismissed this case. div.head: SAVINGS BANK DE'POSIN AND THE PRICE OF CONSOLS.
div.p: SAVINGS BANK DE'POSIN AND THE PRICE OF CONSOLS.

The interesting statements made and evoked by Nit-. Benj trnin Cohen in the debate on the Budget on Thurs. thy with regard to the accumulation of money in thn Post-office Savings Bank deserves more attentinn than they received. An increase of £10,000,000 to the total of the Trustee and Po-t-office Savings Bank together in a single year may not mean in present • trade circum- stances a withdrawal of m mey from the ordinary trad- ing banks of the country,bint it is certainly not a fact to congratulate the taxpayer or the Government upon. for the liabilities of the nation on these deposits is already most onerous,and it is a liability which is incurred at an increasiog risk of loss to the Treasury on every advance in the price of consols. The money of the small saver i 4 invested in Gwereirnmt stock, and mach of the o' 1- in- vestments no doubt stand in the books of the batiks at handsome profit. But the new purchases at 105 to 108 must land the banks in certain loss—in one direction becausa the stock pays them less than they give, and in another because, shauld the time come when stock has to be s ad to pay depositors their money, the SfkieS must be effected at a loss proportioned to the ex- travagance of the price now. For yeirs the Government have been competing, against the savings bank as a buyer , of stock for terminable annuity and sinkinz fund pip-- poses, and latterly the Bank of England has been a third competitor. The price of stock has therefore reached an unprecedented height, and every year promises to force it still higher until the day conws when war or some ;adverse conjunction of credit forces large selling. The price may go down faster than it rose, and sales have to hi- effected to pay depositors 10 per cent, or moro undcr the present price. The moral is that the Govern- ment should not enc mrage deposits so much hv keeping its rate of interest so far above that ot the m trice% and further that the scope for invoqrnents should be widened so as to include the greater home Corporation stocki and perhaps other securi•ies now available for trustees.

OFFICIAL RETURNS oF WESLEYAN MEMBERSHIP.

Last week at the May District Synods held throughout the country, the official completed returns of Church membership, with additional particulars of interest to Wesleyan Methodists, were presented. They now show that twenty-eight of the districts report an increase of 5,511, whilst only five report decrease of I,loB—mak- ing a net gain on the year of 4,374 members. Outside the metropolis there is a distinctly marked line of in- crease along the whole of the Eastern Coast away to Whitby and Darlington. The western districts also shew up well. During the past year 46.043 new mem- bers have been fully received, but from various causes 23,812 have ceased to be recoznlz .1 ss members. The casualties caused by death number 5,290, and the losses by emigrations are 383. The leakage from wear and tear is therefore considerable, despite the precautions adopted to prevent the loss. The full returns are as follows :—ln total membership, 437,724; on trial ditto. 29,885; junior members, 72,678; candidates for the ministry, 122.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. FRIDAY.-THE "TIED ROUSE" QUESTION.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. FRIDAY.-THE "TIED ROUSE" QUESTION.

In the Elouse of Commons on Friday evening last week,on the motion to go into Committee of Supply Mr. KEARLEY moved that it was highly desirable that the terms and conditions of employment in the Post-office should be made the subject of inquiry, with a view to the removal of any reasonable cause of complaint. Mr. A. MORLEY said he was prepared to appoint a committee composed of gentlemen who had sp2cial practical know- ledge and experience of administration, who would, he hoped, be assisted by a member of the Labour Depart- ment of the Board of Trade. There woul4 be one offic;al of the Post-office on the committee, otherwise it would be confined to officials ef the Civil Service who were unconnected with the Post-office.

At the evening sitting, on the motion to go into Com- mittee of Supply, Mr. W. ALLEN moved an amendment affirming that immediate legislation was desirable to put a stop to the system of" tied houses." Mr. BROADHURST I seconded the motion. Mr. EVERSHED (a brewer) admitted the evils of the system. He said he did not think legis- lation this seasm was possible, but they had better appoint a Select Committee than do nothing. After . some further discussion Mr. G. W. RUSSELL said he ! feared that their programme of legislation for this year was full enough. He thought the proposal for a com- mittee of inquiry was too wide,and he could not support it. Between new and the period of the isill of the Govern- ment there would be sufficient time for the investiga- tion ot the subject. The motion for Supply being with- drawn, Mr. ALLEN'S amendment became the substantive motion. Mr. BUCIENILL moved a new amendment in favour of a Committee of Inquiry into the subject. This amendment was defeated by 98 to 59. A motion for the. closure was carried by 91 be 51, but the mai)rity not being sufficient the debate stood adjourned. MONDAY.

In the HOMO of Commons on Mm e 7 eveninz, Mr. MORLEY, replying to Mr. Kiimsaid he equld not promise to find time for the remaining stages of the Coercion Ae.t Repeal Bill. Sir %V. HARCOURT informed Mr. BARTLEY that the Local Veto Bill would certainly bo taken, but not before Whitsuntide.

Mr. J. EIAVELOCK WILSON desired to move the adjourn- ment of the House in order to call attention to the con- ditions of employment of Lascar seamen on licar.l British ships ; but the SPEAK Ea held that such a question did not come within the scope of the standing order. The House again went into Committee ou the Welsh Church Bill. On clause 3, which provides that Welsh ecclesiastical property shall be transferred to certain Commissioners, Mr. LLOYD-GEORGIC moved to substitute " Council "for " Commissioners," desiring to place the administration of the liberated funds in the hands of a joint committee of the county councils. Mr. Aegean:l said he should regard the acceptance of the amendment as fatal to the further progress of the bill. Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE said that if the proposed Com- missioners rejected any scheme there would be no remedy, and he pressed his amendment. Sir G. 0. MORGAN said he would vote against the amendment, not because he disapproved of it, but be- causeit would destroy the Bill. Sir M. HICKS-BEACII supported the amendment. Mr. Asperses said he was willing to reconsider this question when they c4lllO to clause 9, but the Government could not, accept the amendment, and if it was carried it would be his duty to move to repert progress. Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE then said that he would not at this stage press the amend- ment. The Opposition, however, insisted on a division and the Committee divided, with the following remit : For the amendment, 188 ; against, 198 ; Government majority, 10. Other amendments were iejectecl and progress was reported shortly after midnight. in the House of Lords the Earl of JERSEY moved for a Select Committee to inquire into the operation of a pro- viso in the Railway anti Canal rraffic Act, 1888, which directs that for "the same or similar s.irvices" the rates, tolls, or charges for home and foreign merchandise on English railways shall be the same. Be said that the proviso certainly did not intend th ,t preferential rates should be given to foreign merchandise, but in practice imported goods were carried, at through rates froxn the port of arrival to the London. markets, at prices with which it was hopeless for the home producer to attempt to comp-te ; and not only were the rates lower, but quicker trains were provided and greater facilities were given in transit. Lord PLAYMIR said everyone svmpa- thised with the principle that under certain conditions I foreign goods sheuld have no preference in rates of transit over British goods, but it was a different thing to say that foreign and British goods should always be carried at the same rates. It was not for a Select Coin- , tnittee to inquire into the operations of the proviso,which had been decermined already by a court of law, and the Government could not favour the appointment of such a Committee. • The Marquis of SALISBURY pointed out that a decision had been given in a case brought before the Railway Commissioners, but that decision might be I appealed against, and he therefore advised the Earl of JERSEY to consent to the adjournment of the debate until the time for appeal was gone by. The Earl of JERSEY accepted the suggestion, and the debate was formally adjourned. The bill which aims at the suppression of cockfiehting in Scotland was read a second time befire the House rose.

TUESDAY. In the Fiouse of Cornmans on Tuesday evening Mr. CARVELL WILLIAMS drew the attention of the SECRETARY to cite I.)cal Government Board to the inclusion of a voluntary church rate in the poor-rate notes of the township of Manchester. Mr. SHAW-LEFIEVRE said the note stated that the " Church levy " was optional, but he thought it would be better if the item was not included in a demand note for a compulsory rate. _

Sir W. Haricot:Ha brought up the report of the com- mittee on tho case of the Earl of SELBORNE. It simply stated that Lord WormEa had succeeded to the Earldom of Selborne. Mr. ANSTRUTHER (Liberal UM mist Whip) moved for the issue of a writ for the election of a mem- ber for West Edinburgh in room of Lord WOLMER. Mr.C,uazoN said that the House was usurping functions which did not properly belong to it. Those who had supported the Earl of SUBORNS'S contention had not acted without consulting the highest legal authorities. He prophesied that the question would not be allowed to slumber, and that in the reform of the House of Lords which was certain to loom in the near future the eligibility of peers to sit in the House of Commons would not play an unimportant part. Sir W. flaticouter said be had always treated the claim which had been set up as an absurd and almost childish one. Mr. DALZIEL moved the adjournment of the debate, but the motion was defeated by 343 to 10, and the motion for the issue of the writ was agreed to. A bill introduced by Mr. BROADEILITIST to deal with the subject of tied houses was read the first time. WEDNESDAY.

At the clmmencement of public business in the House of Commons on Wednesday, Sir W. HARCOURT moved that no committees should sit to-day (Ascension Day) until two o'clock. Mr. BYLES said be was glad that this annual motion was year by year being passed by smaller m ajorities. It was not an expression of a genuine de- sire ; it was merely a simulation of devotional feeling, and he opposed it in the name of true religion. He moved as an amendment that the Grand Committee on Trade, which was engaged in dealing with the Factories and Worksilopi Bill, should be allowed to sit at the uscal hour. Mr. LEON seconded the amendment. Sir M. H. Sge.ca, censured the language used by Mr. BYI.ES. The only reason for the exemption of a Committee from the operation of the rule was urgency, and there was no urgency about the proceedings of the Grand Commigee. Sir W. HARCOURT cisuld not accept the amendment. He deprecated the introduction of religious questions into the debate, as he was sure that the House was never en ployed to so little advantage as when it allowed ques- tions of relleious difference to become the subject of de- bate. After some further discussion Mr.Bytirs withdrew his a mend ment.a nd the original motion was adopted, on a oi vision, by 94 to 82.

div.head: Eettero to the Obitor.
div.p: Eettero to the Obitor.
THE RECENT FIRE.

Sir,—With regard to the recent fire at Messrs. Skel- ton's shop, we as a body of men think that there has been a great injury dene to our character by the "Observer's Own Spectator " in publishing what he has done in the "Observer." As regards the time the alarm of fire was given, we think that "Observer's Own Spectator" must have been in bed when the alarm was given ad sent one of h's children to get the report for bim for it is only child's talk ; it is not the talk ol a sen- sible person, for he has got in his remarks that the alarm was giken at exactly five o'clock and that it was twenty- two minutes past five when the engine arrived en the scene. According to this we must have been on the "scene with the steamer at exactly seven minutes after the alarm was given, for it was given at exactly quarter past five and there was water on from the mains at 19 minutes past, and the firemen were fighting with the flames inside until the word from our superintendent was given to connect to the steamer and then the full force of water was got on. So he must be a clever man to know about the fire before anyone else.—Signed, THE FIREMEN.
Fire Engine Shed, Warrington.

Sir,—On behalf of the directors and shareholders of W. P. and W. Skelton, Limited, I desire to tender my sincere thanks to the many earnest volunteer workers, who rendered us such valuable services on the occasion of our late fire. To our neighbours, the whole of whom so spontane- ously placed their premises at our disposal, for the pro- tection of rescued stock (so losing the whole of their Friday evening's trade) I feel especially grateful and assure them that their kindness will never be forgotten by faithfully yours, WILLIAM P. SKELTON, Managing Director.

Sir,—Although Warrington is very fortukate in occa- sionally having the ready and valuable help of the Wilderspool and Crosfield's fire engines, it is very pro- bable, as evidenced by the great damage to the Jubilee premises, that the town is very far from a satisfactory position in regard to the saving of property. The War- rington firemen worked hard and with a will according to their lights limited as they are by not over elaborate training, and instead of being roughly criticised as they were by many of the crowd they should receive the reasonable amount of credit which is honestly their due. —Yours truly,
A READER.
THE CATTLE MARKET SCHEME.

was very sorry to see the " Examiner last week supporting the transfer of the Pig Market to the Old Barracks, Bank Quay, because it is a generally ac- cepted rule of Corporations to keep all markets &c.,out of residential districts, and, because tnarkets,never suc- ceed which are scattered in distant parts of the towns instead of being kept as close together as possible. A pig market at Bank Quay cannot succeed because so far from the potato and vegetable market, the resort of pig buyers, to say nothing of the nuisance caused to the Bank Quay district. The reason of the attempt to estab- lish a pig market at the present Technical School is really,l believe,to show that the purchase of the Barracks audits "gift "at cosrprice to the Corporation is not a white elephant. Could not our Mayor further distin- guished his year of office by purchasing and transferring to the Corporation another long offered, and empty block, say near his present residence, for a smallpox hospital and so make this year ever memorable.—Yours truly, [UNBELIEVER IN CORPORATION WISDOM.

Sir,—lt seems to me that in your leader of Saturday last upon this subject yen make several assumptions which have no real basis of fact. For instance,you say that "the opposition to this scheme is not so strong as it was." And yet a memorial bearing upwards of 100 sig- natures of householders in this locality had been pre- sented against the proposal. I have reason to believe that many more names would have appeared in that list, had the memorial been obtained in a more leisurely way. As it is that petition to the Town Council hardly seems an evidence of a weakened opposition to the scheme in question. Then you say that it can "scarcely be doubted that there is a growing feeling that the Barracks are the most suitable site." I have spoken with many of my neighbours on this matter, and I can testify that this feeling is not growing hereabouts. I can quite under- stand that it may be growing in other localities, especi- ally such as have been suggested as alternative situa- tions for this which, as everybody knows, will he a troublesome nuisance, place it where you may. That which nobody cares about having by his own door, everybody thinks would he tar h tter by the door of somebody else. And this, in my opinion, goes to show the folly of placing a cattle market anywhere in the midst of a population. I doubt if a town can he found where in recent times the authorities have had the teme- rity to put down such a market in the midst of the population. These markets are placed properly on the outskirts, where they will be as little nuisance as pos- sible to the majority of the people. And as for the centre of the town being preferable for the sake of the conveni- ence of buyers and sellers, the idea is absurd. Buyers and sellers will be sure to go where they can transact their business. There will only be one cattle market, I presume. There will he no competition, and hence it will be inevitable that farmers and others will go where ever the market is put down. ra The thing to be considered is the welfare of the whole community, not the occasional convenience of cattle dealers and butchers. These gentlemen are no doubt entitled to all reasonable consideration,but when we are told that the purity of our atmosphere,the cleanliness of our streets, the quietness of a residential neighbour- hood are to be sacrificed to the convenience of a handftll of business people who may pay us occasional visits, we are told what we do not admit, very strongly object to. ; and even consider to be absurd. Warrington has no very eminently attractive residen- tial localities. But I suppose that Wilson Patten-street and those adjoining are among the most eligible. And yet the Town Council, in its marvellous collective wis- dom (?) thinks, or seems to think, that for the sake of a cattle market the charawter f this neighbourhood and the value of its property may well be put in jeopardy I I venture to suggest another site, namely Palmyra. square itself. That is the only plaasant bit ot open space hereabout, arid in this utilitarian age it seems a pity that decent houses should have anything pleasant to look at. Therefore put the cattle pens, and the pig pens down in that space. It can no doubt be bought for a price, and the money can come out of the rates. The thing would be about as sensible as the present scheme. Only the difficulty is, as we all know,that the Barracks have been bought, and as they have been bought they must be put to some use. I have never yet properly understood whether the purchase of this pro- perty was discussed by the Council before or after it was carried out ? If before, I do not recollect seeing any report of it, and if after, why discussion was too late. I hope, however, that it fis not too late to stop this precious scheme. It is quite bad enough to be exposed to the increasing dirt and din of the railway,and the noxious fumes from works at Bank Quay, without having tins added nui- sance both to nose and ears that will inevitably attend the opening of a Cattle Market here, and the collecting of animals, and their necessary drovers and keepers,who among them will make it very lively indeed. By the way, if Palmyra Square does not suit, why not try the neighbourhood of the Latchford Railway Station? The railway accommodation is good, and all the needful public-house accommodation could sodh ba provided. Yours faithfully, 19, Wilson Patten-street, May 15, 1895.
JOHN YONGE.
PEACE AT ANY PRICE-IF REASONABLE.
Sir,—l asked the gentleman to state what he meant by peace at any price. He answered it was a silly ques- tion to ask, and he further tells us that he would not

have war on any consideration whatever, in which case lam bound to say that be is very foolish. Our trade is very bad now, and at the present time the Government have to show the greatest determination and firmness consistent with peace, to save it from being a great deal worse. If our friend is weak let him find consolation in the Bible; if he is strong let him find encouragement from the same source. We are not Christs but human beings, and a e are bound to use all our forces as humanely as we can, and like the fighting parson turn the other cheek, but when they have the rank audacity to strike the second blow punish them as they so richly deserve, and the Bible in that one particular does not say that we may not. Behold, I will take all the families of the north saith the Lord,and Nebuchadrezzir the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will ut- terly destroy them,and make them an astonishment,and an hissing, and perpetual desolations." Jeremiah, xTlv. 9.—Yours truly,
A READER.

div.head: PEACE AT ANY PRICE.
div.p: PEACE AT ANY PRICE.

Sir,—Whether your correspondent with a Latin name is a church or chapel man, or an unbeliever I know not; but his letter shows that courtesy is not one of his strong points. The application of such elegant phrases as "twaddle" and "pietistic cranks" to people who are deeply impressed with the conviction that war under any circumstances is an outrage upon the government of the world, and an unspeakable wrong to mankind, is quite unworthy of a gentleman whose education enables him to quote Latin. The question at issue, however, is not whether the advocates of peace are "pietistic cranks" or not ; but whether the wholesale slaughtering of human beings for any cause, or no cawe at all, is consistent with Christianity? 01 course, if our Latin friend regards the founder of that religion as a "mytho- logical personage" I am not prepared to discuss the war question with him, as such a discussion might only gen- der strife, and perhaps lead to the suspicion that his facts and his reasoning partook, in some measure, of the spirit of that other "mythological personage" who is described in an ancient writing as "a murderer from the beginning." But what a wide field lies before our friend for the display of his talent in another direction! How scath- ingly and righteously he might denounce the hollow sham of a people calling themselves Christians who are groaning under a war debt of 660 millions, and continue to spend many millions a year on military equipments? He might tell as, too, that the wars of this " Christian " country have not all been waged for defensive purposes; for since the days of the Spanish Armada no nation has ever attempted to land a soldier upon our shores. He knows very well that we have carried fire and sword in every quarter of the earth for the avowed purpose of promot- ing British interests and the spread of the splendid civi- lization which savours so strongly of the beer barrel and the rum bottle. And waxing warm with his subject he might expose the hypocrisy of the priests in reaping a golden harvest every year tor preaching peace and bless- ing war from the same pulpits. But after all, our learned friend may be a Christian of some sort for the nom de guerre under which he conceals his identity indicates that he is prepared to fight for his altar and his home. Now let me humbly =aka a sug- gestion to him before he puts on his armour. Let him try by the standard of the New Testaments wheTher war is consistent with his profession as a Christian man,and if he finds that it is, let the result be published in the " Examiner," and Ifor one will give it a respectful and impartial hearing. " The Boys' Brigade" to which your correspondent refers is, from my point of view, another development of the diabolism whi3h exists amongst us and is,as might be expected. under the wing of " The Churcn." That venerable offspring from the hoary and blood-stained popery of pat times is quite consistent with her origin and traditions when she declares that it is lawful for Christian men at the command of the magistrate, to carry weapons and serve in the wars. , This diabolical proposition may suit the state, establishment of religion but it finds no support in the Christian code which for- bids fighting under any pretence whatever.—Yours truly.

div.head: PEACE AT ANY PRICE.
div.p: PEACE AT ANY PRICE.

Sir,—Your Jingo correspondent " Pro aria et focis " in attempting to show the other side of what he regards as the "twaddle " on the above subject, unconsciously pro- ceeds to write the veriest twaddle himself. He says that if England adopted the doctrine of non-resistance to aggression, the Society of Friends would quickly lose the platform from which they preach this peculiar doctrine. Now, in making an assertion of this kind " Pro aria et focis "shows that he does not know what is going on in the world. One might take it for granted that the one country of the world in which the doctrine of non- resistance would flourish least would be Russia, where the government is of such an autocratic character. Yet, strange to say, in this benighted country, the doctrine finds its sturdiest opponents, and the cause flmrishes in spite of the extreme measures adopted to suppress it. In studying his Bible, the Russian peasant finds, what many of Us English Chris- tians have discovered, that war is at variance with the teachings of Jesus Christ, and therefore he will have none of it, cost what it may. To the realization of this fact we wish to bring the English people, and so long as we have tongues in our heads and people to speak to we shall never lack a platform. Personally, I never could get behind the rank hypoc- risy of the English people. Professing ta be followers of Christ, and to regulate their lives by His Word, which forbids killing, and stealing, and inculcites many obligations to our neighbours and weaker brethren, whenever the English see any opportunity of self ag- grandisement their professions go to the wall,aNd the real men display themselves. Of what avail is it then for the poor Ashantees, the Zulus, the Matabele, the Mashonas, and other people's throughout the world to cry " Pro aria et focis 1" What respect have we for their altarsand their hearths ? They are only ignorant blacks to be trampled (down, and " bossed" by that superior creature the Britisher,who, when he has broken down their altars and laid their hearths in ruins, pro- ceeds to introduce to the " niggers " the Bible to save their souls, and fire water to destroy their bodies. Is it not time that the Christian people of this land who have the lighr, proclaimed it to those who still pit in darkness? When we lolly realize the teaching of Jesus Christ on the subject of war, we cease to be patriots, and recognise the universal brctherhood of man.—Your3 &e.
A CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOURER.

div.head: PEERS AND THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
div.p: PEERS AND THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

The. Select Committee appointed by the House of Commons to inquire into the circ,anstances under which a new writ was issued for the Attercliffe division of shertietd on the succession of the Hon. Bernard Colo- ridge to the peerage has presented a first report on the question how far the succession to a peerage affects the status of a member of the House of Commons. They find that succeeding to a peerage disables the person so succeeding from being elected to or from sitting or vot- ting in the House of Commons. They also declare that when a member has succ sled to a peerage and delays or refuses to apply for a writ of summons to the House of Lords, the House of Commons is entitled, and may in the interest of the constituency be bound, to ascertain the fact of the succession by such inquiry and upon such evidence as it considers appropriate to the case.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.

A meeting of the Runcorn Free Library Committee was held in Town Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday even- ing. There were present : Rev. J. Simpson, Messrs. W. Handley, W. J. Cunningham, U. J. Hrice, T. Riley, W. Hankinson, S. Pope,and Mr..). D. Jones (lihrarian).

div.head: CHAIRMAN AD VICE-CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN AD VICE-CHAIRMAN.

Mr. Riley proposed, and Mr. Pope seconded, that Mr. William Handley he re-appointed the chairman of the committee. The motion wascarried unanimously.—The Chairman in taking the chair said he was much obliged to the members for electing him again chairman for the second or third time. He always took a great deal of in- terest in the work, and with their co-operation the duties had been very light and agreeable. He had every reason to believe that in the coming year he would have a continuance of that support, and that their meetings would be attended with success.—Mr. U. J. Once was appointed vice-chairman, on the motion of Mr. Hankiu- son, seconded by Mr. Pope.

REPORT OF THE LIBRARIAN. The report of the Librarian (Mr. Jones) showed that there had been issued during the month 1,909 volumes distributed as follows :—Theology 22, philosophy 10, science 70, history Stc. 129, poetry 18, fiction 1,510, mis- cellaneous 139, French literature 4, and music 9. This was an increase of 169 on the corresponding period last year. In the reference department the issues were 35, or an increase of three on last year.

div.head: GIFTS TO THE LIBRARY.
div.p: GIFTS TO THE LIBRARY.

The following gifts were reported :—By Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., several Bills before Parliament, Parlia- mentary reports, and reports of the Commissioners con- cerning charities (Cheshire) ; library reports from Ash- ton-under-Lyne, Great Yarmouth, uosport, Ealing, Shoreditch, Bootle, Wimbledon, and Hanley ; from Mr. Ernest Mason (the author) " WonaanhoA in the Good- man "; from Mr.E.Burgis (the author) "Perils to British ['rade" ; anonymously, " tho Work of the Holy Spirit," sermon by the Rev. S. C. Lowry ;and by Mr.W.R.Wass, the Popular Encyclopoelia, 14 volumes, Special men- tion was made to the gifts of Mr. Wass and Mr. Brunner.
FINANCE. It was resolved to ask the Council to pay £5O to the library account as a portion of the amount due from the penny rate. There was no other business of public interest.

In the Divorce Division on Tuesday, Mrs. Mabe Grindley Power obtained a decree of judical separation on the ground of the adultery of her husband, Philip Ernest Power. • The parties were married at Dunham Massey, Cheshire, in 1883.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 25, 1895
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 25, 1895
EARLESTOWN ,IND 'NEWTON.
HAYDOCK PARISH CHURCH.

Special services were held in t-h—e-a:hove church on Sunday in aid of the church building debt. Instructive sermons were preached by the Rev. Canon Whittington, M.A., rector of Orsett and Rural Dean. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, NEWTON.

It will be seen from an advertisement that the anniversary services in aid ot the Sunday school connected with the above church will take place on Sunday. In the afternoon a musical service will be given, and the pulpit at the morning and evening services will be occupied bN the Rev. Herber Evans, the popular Welsh divine and Principal of Bangor College.

div.head: STEALISG ON THE MAILICET PLACE.
div.p: STEALISG ON THE MAILICET PLACE.

At the Town Hall. Newton, on Saturday morning, before Mr. Borrom Mary Ann Bradley, of Common- road, Newton, was charged with stealing a child's pinafore the previous night from a stall on the Market place, the property of Albert Peacock, of Warrington. She was remanded to the Sessions on Saturday.

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE.
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

On Wednesday evening the usual meeting of the Samuel Morley section ot Ca lets was held in the Co-operative Hall at 7 o'clock, Bro. Judson, W.P., presided. Two new members were proposed. About 50 members were present. At 8 o'clock the Britain's Need Division met in the same room, Bro. S. Foden,W.P. Presiding,after opeqing business one new member was initiated. Reports were given by the delegates on the Pic-nic Committee, who stated that arrangements were completed for visit- ing Frodsham on July 6th. After other routine business had been transacted a pleasant meeting was closed at 9.30.

div.head: 1.0.G.T. (EBENEZER LODGE)..
div.p: 1.0.G.T. (EBENEZER LODGE)..

The usual weekly session of the Eirlestown Ebenezer Lodge was held in the Co-operative Hell, on Tuesaay. The session was presided over by Bro. Brown,C.T.; there being a good attendance of mem- bers and friends. Bro. W. J. Taylor read the dis- trict lodge circular stating that the district lodge would be held at Southport on Saturday next, and representatives were instructed accordingly. Bro. John Taylor then gave a Lancashire reading. Sister Coombs was responsible for the programme, and a very interesting evening was spent, the members and friends enjoying themselves very heartily with the good things provided.

div.head: EARLESTOWN BAPTIST SUNDAY SCHOOL
div.p: EARLESTOWN BAPTIST SUNDAY SCHOOL

The special anniversary services in aid of the above school, were held in the Baptist Chapel on Sunday. Special hymns were sung by the choir and children, and the services were conducted morning and evening by the Rev. Carey Bonner, of Sale,who preached appropriate discourses to large congrega- tions, In the afternoon a cantata "The blessing of the children," was excellently rendered by the children and choir, assisted by Misses Mee and Eckersley, Messrs. G; W. Kidd and W. Limond. The choir also sang thi- anthem "0 Lord our Governer," Miss Mee taking the solo. Mr. E. Eckersley pre- sided at the organ, and Mr. S. liarvey conducted. A short address was also given by the Rev. C. Bonner. The collection during the day amounted to over £34. EARLESTOWN TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION CLASSES.

The results of the examinations in practical cookery,- and laundry recently held in connection with the above classes have been received as fol- lows :—Cookery ; Miss S. Percival Ist class ; Misses S. Warburton, and A. K. Wood; Ist. class ; Miss L. Boardman, Mrs. J. H. Emmett, Misses A. Harrison, A. Judson and E. Naylor, 2nd class ; Misses L Chandley, A. Hill, and A. Ilulme, 3rd class. Laun- dry, Mrs. J. H. Emmett, Misses M. R. Thompson, R. Alderson, N. Childs, Ist. class; Nlisses A. H. Jackson, E. Mather, S. Percival, M. Birks, 2nd class.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge ot Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, on Monday evening. Bro. W. Wilson presided, and there was a good attendance of mem- bers and officers of No. 1 Convention, including Bros. Roberts (Warrington),Francis (St. Helens),and Taylor. The programme for the quarter was sub- mitted and adopted. The summary of the Grand Lodge Sessions was read by Bro. Newman, L.D. The meeting was afterwards declared open, Bro. G. Clarke being responsible for the programme, which consisted of songs, recitations, readings' &c., given by Messrs. W. H. Crowther, Wilson, and Clarke, and Sisters Newman and Jones. A resolution in favour of the Direct Veto Bill was adopted. STEALING} FROII A CHILD AT EARLESTOWN.

At the Town ii.all, Newton, on Wednesday morning before Mr. C. B. F. Borron John Bain- bridge, a sailor, belonging to Whitby, Yorkshire, was charged with stealing three shillings from a child named Plant, three years of age, on Tuesday. The prisoner had been staying with the child's parents in Grafton-street and Mrs. Plant on Tues- day morning sent the child with three shillings to pay the rent. She asked the prisoner to accompany the child into Market-street, which he did, but as the child did not return, she sent her daughter to look for it. She found it wandering about Market- street and ascertained that Bainbridge had taken the money. Mr. Plant then set off in the direction of Warrington, and overtook the prisoner in a brewer's dray on his way to the latter place. He charged him with taking the money, and the prisoner at once admitted it, and said tie did not know what had possessed him to take it, and pro- duced 2s. :211., having spent the balance of the money. Plant brought him back to Earlestown and handed him over to the police. Prisoner was remanded to the sessions on Saturday. EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The 138.1- quarterly meeting of the Earlestown Co-operative Society was held in the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening. Mr.. J. Moss presided, and there was a lair attendance of members. The report and statement of accounts showed that the cash receipts for goods sold during the quarter amounted to £4,331 3e. 61 The net profit avail- able for dividend was £506 Ile. 7id., which would allow of a dividend of 21. 31. in the £ to members, and Is. Id. in the A,' on the purchases of non-mem- bers, leaving a balance of £9 us, 241. to be added to the Contingent fund. During the quarter 15 new members had been admitted and 36 had withdrawn or been struck off the books, the present member- ship on the books being 1,007, of whom 723 had brought in checks. Messrs. D. Barcroft and T. Swift were appointed Committee men, and Mr. J. Jones was re-elected stock-taker. The subject .of the employes annual picnic was brought up, and it was decided to make a grant of 7s. 61. to each ser- vant, for the purpose of enabling them to have a picnic at the expense of the Society. The usual grant of £5 to she Technical Instruction classes was made. It was also decided to make a grant of .E 1 Is. to the.Diglake colliery disaster fund. The question of new ovens was brought up, the Chair- man stating that the Committee .had accepted tender to erect new hot air ovens at a cost of £144.
THE CHEMICAL TRADE AT RUNCORN.
LETTER FROH THE UNITED ALIKALI__COMPANY„

Mr. Eustace Carey, wri ing from the United Alkali Company's Offices on day 21st to Mr. Marshatl, secre- tary of the Runcorn Urban Council, said—" Your Couu- cil's memorial, dated the 23rd ult., has been carefully considered by the directors of this Company, and I am requested to assure you that the closing or partial clfss- ing of any of our works is a matter of great regret to the directors, but that the necessity fur such a course has been brought about ts a large extent by the general depression of trade, which is entirely beyond our con- trol, and also by improvements and economies which we have effected, and which enable us to considerably in- crease the output from the machinery and plant that which we have at work. It therefore has been neces- sary to close or partially close some of our works, and in deciding which works should be stopped the directors have corsidered the prosperity of the Company as a whole and have taken the course which they believed to be taken in the interests of our shareholders, which must always be our 'main object. The directors wish me also to inform you that no efforts will be spared to keep our Runcorn works going as far as practicable,and , they hope that with the revival of trade, and possibly ' some new departures these works will not in the long run suffer teeny great extent. I may remind you t hat a large number of men living in Runcorn work in Wid- nes, and we have by adopting what is known as the " eight hours shift " found employment for a consider- able number of extra hands."

It will be remembered that a deputation from the , Runcorn Council waited upon Mr. Brock a short time ago with the memorial referred to, which was published in these Columns, and it was then promised that a reply would be sent after the meeting of the directors. Rum- ours have been rife during the week as to the proposed commencement of new works at Weston Point, but with regard to this, nothing definite has been necided upon. Enquiries are being made by the Birmingham Company who it is supposed are thinking of commencing a new industry in the locality, but they have not yct decided to do so.
One hundred all thirtjtivo miners who wer, en- tombed in the Monongahell mine, West Vir4iaia, Lave been rescued alive.

div.head: DROWNING OF A BOATMAN AT
div.p: DROWNING OF A BOATMAN AT
RUNCORN.

A COMPLIMENT TO THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY. A boatman named Edward Beans of the flat Gertrude, was drowned in a lock at Runcorn on Friday night. Mr. J. E. Worslek, coroner, held an inquest at the Cemetery office on Monday afternoon, relative to the death of the deceased. The first witness called was Marzaret Beans, wife of the deceased, who stated that deceased was a boatman on the flat Gertrude, belonging to the Ship Canal Com- pany. She lived on board with him. He was 40 years of age last April. She last saw him alive on Friday about 10.30 when he was going over the bridge at Bottom Locks with a man named Frederick Leavenswood. He seemed sober at the time but she did not speak to him. James Burns, captain of the flat Gertrude, on which the deceased was "hand," deposed that Beans had been with him about six weeks. Deceased did not take much drink. On Friday they were loading near the crate warehouse at Runcorn, and finished doing so about 830. Witness, deceased, and a man named Leavenswood afterwards went to the Duke of Wellington Inn. The deceased had two glasses of whiskey. He did not have any in the afternoon so far as witness knew. They afterwards went towards the boat. On the way, they reached a field, the deceased pulled off his jacket and wanted to fight. Witness thought it was ,a joke, and took deceased's clothing to the boat, leaving the deceased with Leavens- wood. About 20 minutes afterwards witness was told that there Was something in the lock. He assisted in the search for the body. He did not think it dangerous for a man in drink to cross the locks, certainly not the two top ones by which the deceased might cross. The deceased had been a boatman all his life time. In answer to a question by a juryman witness did not think de- ceased and Leavenswood had had time to go back to the Wellington" again. Cross-examined by Inspector Flicks, the witness stated that the deceased after having had the whiskies,left him and Leavenswood at the public house, to go to purchase something. When he returned he had a small Iwhiskey. Witness had forgotton that. In answer to another question by the Inspector, witness said it was before Leavenswood came to offer to help him with the boat that he had heard a man was iu the lock. _ _

Edward Williams stated that he was taking his flat through the bottom locks at Runcorn about 10.30 on Friday night when he saw the deceased. He was then standing near to the middle gates. There was no one with him. It was dark at the time. A few minutes afterwards he heard cries of ''Ned" coming from the I lock. Witness got a rope and threw it in the water but cluld not see anyone. He afterwards saw the body I recovered. Frederick Leavenswood, captain of the Aline, belong- ing to the Manchester Ship Canal Conapany,said he had , not known the deceased for very long. On Friday even- ing be, with the deceased and Burns, went to have a drink at the " Wellington." Witness felt all right on leaving the public-house, but when he got into the fresh air he tumbled over. He could not say whether the de- ceased was drunk or sober. Witness corroborated Burns' statement as to the deceased wanting to fight, and stated that he left him at the foot of the bridge leading over Francis dock. Witness then went to assist Burns in bringing his boat to the middle lock, and afterwards proceeded to his own boat. He did not know anything about the deceased getting into) the water until next morning. P.C. Richardson stated tnat the body was given into his charge. He examined the body,but did not find any marks of violence. He found is. op. in the deceased's pockets. There was no sign of a struggle having taken place at the locks. The Coroner said on the face of it the case seemed sur- rounded with a great deal of mystery, but in all proba- bility the three men were under the influence of drink at the time, and he thought the verdict to be returned should be one of "Found drowned." This the jury de- cided upon. Referring to an inquest which was held on the body of a child that was drowned at the Top Pool a short time ago, the Coroner stated that a presentment was made by the jury which was supported by himself, that the railings surrounding the pool, were, considering the number of children trespassers, in a dangerous state. It was presented to the local agent of the Ship Canal Com- pany and the place had now been made perfectly secure, and he thought there would be a difficulty for a child to get to the pool again. He thought it was most satis- factory that the recommendations were so well carried out by the Ship Canal Company.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT.

At last the Runcorn Urban Council have received a reply to their memorial to the United Alkali Com- pany. It is not a particularly hopeful one but still on the whole it is as satisfactory as many expected. The director's account for the closing or partial closing of any of their works by the general depres- sion of trade and by improvements and economies which had been effected and which have enabled them to increase the output. In taking the action they had done with regard to the Runcorn works they state that it was in the best interests of the shareholders of the Company. They affirm that no efforts will be spared to keep their works at Run- corn going as far as practicable, and hope that with the revival of trade, and possibly some new depar- ture, these works will not in the long run suffer to to any great extent. This may be considered a candid and straightforward way of stating their case, but it is to be hoped that the "passible new departures " will soon become actual facts.

There can be no doubt that the formation of the chemical syndicate has had a deleterious effect upon the trade of Runcorn, proving on the other hand, beneficial to Widnes. This, Mr. Carey admits in his letter, for he states that in consequence of the com- pany adopting the eight hour shift they had found employment for a considerable number of extra )ands at Widnes. In order to show that Runcorn receives some little benefit from this, he points out that a large number of their Widnes em- plov6s live in Runcorn. It may be advantageous to Runcorn to be used as a residential quarter by Widnes workmen in their efforts to get away from the grime and chemical fumes of that town, to more salubrious Runcorn, but the percentage of workers doing so is small, and it is safe to say that some of them were previously employed at the Runcorn works. Happily there is nothing in the letter to indicate that the Company's establishments in Runcorn are to be closed entirely and with the present signs of improvement in trade there may be truth in the optimistic view taken by some, that the worst is now over and that brighter times are in store for Runcorn.

A rumour has been current in the neighbourhood during the past week that new works are shortly to be commenced in the district, and Weston Point has been mentioned as being the place where such a development is to take place. This rumour, it may be stated, is rather premature at present, for nothing definite in the way indicated has been decided upon. Negotiations with a view to estab- lishing an entirely new industry in the district have certainly been opened by a Birmingham firm but that is all at present, and it will be some little while before any site is decided upon. Weston Point has many natural advantages which should commend it as a manufacturing centre, and these will no doubt be fully considered by the manu- facturers in question. Should Weston Point be selected, Runcorn will benefit to a great extent— especially the tradesmen, to 4whom increased business would be most welcome.

Not much interest has yet been manifested in the little election that is pending in Runcorn. The vacancy is caused by the bankruptcy gf Councillor Williams who represented Newtown ward on the Urban Council. Several candidates have been ' spoken of as likely to contest the seat but the only candidate who has prepared his address to the electors is Mr. Reynolds who, it will be remem- bered, contested the ward last November and was defeated by a narrow majority by Mr. Williams. Whoever succeeds in the present contest will only be entitl ad to sit in the Council until the next elec- tion of councillors, and this may be the stumbling- block with some persons in coming forward to con- test the seat on the present occasion. The election has been fixed for Saturday, June 15th, and the last date for receiving nominations is the 2:)th inst.

The Muzzling of Dogs' Order was on Wednesday enforced at Runcorn and in several other adjoining districts. Those who would dispute the necessity of such a procedure need only recall the number of cases of moles which have occurred quite recently. It may be considered a punishment to the dogs in having their mouths caged continually, but " pre- ventioki is better than cure" and the muzzling order appears to be the best method of stamping out hydrophobia. It is evident that the animals resent the treatment, for on Wednesday it was quite a novel sight to see them in their endea- vours to rid themselves of the unwelcome muzzles.

A cotton warehouse at Bootle, owned by Alderman J. Webster, and stocked with over 4,000 bales of cotton belonging to Messrs. Paton and Maclaren,was destroyed by fire on Wednesday mulling, the damage being estim- ated at between £40,000 and £50,000.

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES—WARRINGTON. ST. LUKE'S CHURCH. The annual sermons in aid of the Sunday schools were preached in St. Luke's Church, on Sunday, the pulpit, morning and afternoon being occupied by the Rev. EL R. Wild, M.A., and in the evening by the Rev. H. I. Wadeson, rector of Croft. There were good congrega- tions at each service. SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHURCH. The anniversary services in connection with the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Sunday School were held on Sunday, when the preacher morning and evening was the Rev. J. G. Bennett, Wesleyan Connexional Evangel- ist. The services were very successful, and in the even- ing every available inch of space was occupied, and large numbers of people could not obtain admission, and were compelled to return borne. Two excellent sermons were preach by Mr. Bennett, and special hymns were sung by the choir and children. In the afternoon a sacred cantata, entided " The ruler's daughter " was given by an augmented choir with orchestral accom- paniment. Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., presided. The vari- ous pieces were given in a high class manner, and the soloists, &c., were Mrs. Bailey, Miss H. Brough, Miss Armstrong, Mr. Abdy, and Mr. Fanshaw. Mr. Levi Richardson had promised to take the tenor pieces, but was unable to take part owing to indisposition, and thanks are due to Mr. Abdy for coming at so little notice to fill the vacant place. The choir was under the con- ductorship of Mr. W. Brougb, and Mr. T. Brou,gh pre- sided at the organ. The services were continued on Monday night, when the Rev. J. G. Bennett gave a lecture on " To and Fromn Modern Methodism," which we give elsewhere. Collections were taken at each service, and the total amount taken was £25 13.4. 11d., which included £3 lls. 80. collected from the children of the Sunday 5ch001:,,...

- WYCLIFFE P.S. A. The very large attendance at the "open meeting" in connection with the above-named society on Sunday afternoon was evidence—if any were needed—of the popularity of the P.S.A. in Warrington. The president of the society, the Rev. J. Yon,go, was the chairman,and he was accompanied in the pulpit by Mr. F. A. Smith, J.P., of Maxichester. The proceedings commenced with the singing of a hymn which was most heartily engaged in by the congregation. A portion of scripture was then read by Mr. Joseph Garner, and this was followed by the singing of the hymn commencing " 0 Christ in Thee my soul hath found" by Mr. W. H. Wallington. Mr. Healey afterwards engaged in prayer, at the conclusion of which, the Lord's Prayer was sung by the congrega- tion. A quartette entitled "Yea though I walk through the valley of the Shadow of Death " was most efficiently rendered by Mr. and Mrs. R. H. Pearson, Mr. W. H. Wallington and Miss F. Booth. The Chairman briefly introduced the speaker for the afternoon, Mr. Smith J.P., who delivered a pointed address. He urged his hearers to make their homes happy and indicated several ways of doing so, referring to a number of evils to be avoided. In conclusion he spoke of the importance of a good character, stating that if they could not leave their children vast fortunes, they could leave behind them the character of lacing good men and wpmen. Mrs. R. H. Pearson exquisitely sang, " Come unto Me." The Rev. J. Yonge appealed to his hearers for a generous collection towards the expenses of the society, stating that at the open meetings collections were taken inasmuch as the "Chancellors of the Ex- chequer " were present. He also asked the women to sign the Polyglot Petition which is to be presented to Parliament in June. Thc pronouncing of the benedic- ion concluded an essentially religious meeting.

On Wednesday morning, Elizabeth Cbarnock, 49 Napier-st., was found lying in the coal place of her residence, in a dying condition. She was removed hat expired shortly after. Earlier in the morning she appeared to be in her usual health. Dr. Hall, who was called in, certified that death was due to heart disease, and therefore no inquest has been held. On Monday noon a man named William Chadwick, of Lord-street, Chorley, was admitted to the War- rington Infirmary suffering from serious injury to his head and with both his legs fractured. The man was driving a horse and cart along Knutsford- roads, near to Black Bear Bridge, when the animal became startled and ran away. Chadwick was thrown forcibly to the ground whilst endeavouring to control the frightened horse, his head coming into contact with a hard substance. div.head: BIG SCORING BY A WARRINGTON VOLUNTEER.
div.p: BIG SCORING BY A WARRINGTON VOLUNTEER.

A trial competition was held at Altcar on Satur- day, preparatory to the selection of representatives from the Warrington Volunteers, at Bisley. The Delegates' Competition in connection with the Ist Liverpool Rifle Volunteers, for a silver claret jug (value 30 guineas) was also held, and in this com- p..tition Private George Watmough made the remarkable total of 101 out of the possible 105 points, viz.: 34 at 200 yards, 35 at 500 yards, and 32 at GOO yards. This shoot, considering the weather being boisterous, and having a strong changeable right and right rear wind to contend against, must be reckoned as the record of the year 1895, so far as it has advanced. Officers and men alike were unanimous in their congratulations with regard to th 3 performance. It is rather remarkable that this samg shot, made 100 out of the possible 105 exactly 11 year ago when shooting for Lord Winmarleigh's prize on the same range during the Altcar meeting.

div.p: IMPE RIAL PARLIAMENT, Continued from page 3. THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening Sir W. HARCOURT said on Monday and Tuesday they would take the Welsh Church Bill, and he hoped to get the Naval Works Bill into the proceedings of one of the two evenings. He was afraid that unless he could come to some understanding the latter Bill would have to go over. In the course of a subsequent statement Sir WILLIAM said the Government proposed to constitute a Grand Committee for Scotch business generally. They intended to proceed with the Crofters Bill in the House, and would use their best exertions to pass it into law. The House went into Committee on the Finance Bill. On clause 4 Mr. J.LOWTHER proposed that no additional duty should be leviable upon worts made wholly from home grown barley and hops. Mr. GOSCHEN said he could not support the amendment, but be appealed to the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER to forego the extra sixpence on beer. Sir W.HARCOURT said he was notgoing to sacrifice the revenue for the sake of a little cheap populari'y. The.amendment was rejected by 190 to 61. Mr. BARTLEY moved an amendment giving relief from income tax in certain classes of married women's in- come. The amendment was defeated by 144 to 56. Pro- gro.is was reported, and the House resumed. The motion for the appointment of a Standing Com- mittee on Scotch bills was, with some amendment, agreed to. The second reading of the High Court (Lancashire Sitting.) Bill was moved, but objection being taken, it had to be postponed until Tuesday.
