div.head: SATURDAY MORNING.
div.p: SATURDAY MORNING.

Half-past six was striking, and the tramp of feet beneath the window,pro3laimed the passing of the early workers from the suburbs. Hastily swallowing a cup of coffee, I hurried out into the street. The work- people had disappeared and a single labourer, his basket of tools slung over his shoulder, was the only human being in sight. My path lay through a broad strcet, with tall houses standing back in shady gardens. The morning air blowing fresh and pure, from the open country beyond the spacious pleasure park invigorated me, and I seemed to scarcely touch the ground. Further on the streets were narrower, and factories and public- houses disputed with each other for every corner. A , confused hum, and the whirring of machinery, told that the day's work had begun. A sharp turning and an abrupt descent, brought me to my destination, a great building with an handsome front on the public thoroughfare, and two wings at the back, the factory and warehouse. A coal cart was drawn across the narrow street and two men were dis- charging its contents into a cellar beneath the factory wall ; a group of little children hovering near to secure the small pieces which overshot the grating. The nose of the big patient horse touched the opposite side of the street, but he and I were good friends, and he raised his head to allow me to pass. I ought to have entered by the big gateway, but, to save time, I slipped through a small door leading into a long dark passage. There was a window, but it was nearly hidden behind huge bales, and a constant use of this surreptitious entrance, had made me perfectly familiar with its sharp corners and steps in unexpected places. A flight of winding stairs brought me to a large room, filled with counter men, sorting and packing; a second Bight of stairs with a handy balustrade terminated in my own workroom. Outside the door Pierre was handling a sweeping brush, "Late again," she exclaimed, reversing the handle and giving me a vicious dig in the side. " No- thing to do with you," I gasped, seizing a sprinkling can , half filled with water, and retaliating. With a hasty promise to black my eyes at some future time, Pierre beat an ignominious retreat.' hung up my hat and jacket and followed her. Up went Kittum's nose as I passed her machine. " Late again," was all she deigned to say. Sweep opened her mouth, but I started to work at a fearful rate, and drowned her voice and not a sound was heard until half-past eight, wben the born sounded for breakfast and the machinery stopped. Pierre who had hung her wet blouse, a gay pink one, over the gas stove to dry, eyed me resentfully as she slipped it on. " How smart some people are," said Sweep pausing, frying pan in hand, to look at her. " Yours is nearly as smart" Pierre replied, adding in a musing kind of tone, " when its.clean." " Freda, Miss North wants you." "What have I done now." I asked resignedly. " Nothing ; it's something you've left un- done I think." " Oh, very well, say that I'm coming." I felt dAant and lingered, tying my shoe strings into an elaborate bow. Back came the messenger, " She says, Are yo d coming, or is she to come and fetch you 2' The bare possibility made me jump, "Oa, good gracious I'm coming. What can I have done or left undone ?" Five minutcslater I returned in a peculiarly vicious frame of mind and flung myself into a seat. " What's up, Freda," said Kittums, "You look knocked out of time. Been on the carpet ?," I nodded. "What on earth for." "1 left a warm iron on her table and it marked her new oil cloth. She says I've no brains at all." " Who told her you had," said Kittunss. laying down her cup. " Pear's Soap have you been telling tales " ? Pierre shook her head emphatically. " Sit down, Freda," said Molly pulling me back into my chair, "Your breakfast will be cold."

" be even with them vet," I muttered, but Kit- turns heard me. " Freda," she said solemnly "If vim let your angry passions rise you will find yourself at the Town Hall and the Bench will say, Freda, Freda. Your little hands were never made To scratch another's eyes." I sat in disgusted silence, revolving half-a•dozen schemes of vengeance. Steam stopped at twelve o'clock on Saturdays. to allow of machines being cleaned. Each girl swept out her own place, amidst the vigorous pro- tests of her neighbours who could hardly be seen for the dust.

- 'Freda," said Azubah, as I tried to reduce my own particular chair to a superficial tidiness, " Will you draw nity money for me." She handed me the chrue, bearing her number, and I ran off in the wake of Kittums and the others leaving Azubah loosening her hair, for she bad to catch the two o'clack train, and she W3S a tidy soul. The counting house was crowded, for everybody was anxious to be paid, and get away, so I leaned over the balustrade and waited for my turn. Presently Ginger sauntered up With his usual idle air, and balanced him- self upon the lower rail. . . . . .

" Freda, I am going to leave ; going in partnership with my uncle." "I wish you success," I said, for II liked Ginger in spite of his conceit and his silky red hair, " But you mustn't call me Freda now, you know." He stroked his faint moustache and fixed his eyes on a drooping flower at my throat, one %Mums had given me for a peace offering. " That poor flower had a much right to live as you have." "No, it had n't,"ls snapped, " I earn my own living which it never did." 6, Case' of the survival of the fittest," said Ginger ami- ably, aa I left him.

" Azubab, will you reckon your book again," I asked when back in the workroom, " I'm a penny short." "Now, Freddie," said Kittums, shaking at me the finger of reproof, "you know youv'e kept it back for chocolate." "Never mind, Freda," said Azubah, as she buttoned her Sunday jacket. , "It isn't worth the trouble." "It is," I said decidedly, " Kittums shan't be allowed to filch from me my good name. What does twice nineteen make ?" "Thirty-six," said Molly promptly. "Thirty-six pence is three shillings," I cast my eyes over the other columns, "Why, Azubah,,instead of owing you a penny. I've paid you one too many." " Clubs," shouted Sweep, knocking on the table, "Come and pay your club money. Where's Pierre ?" "Gone home," I said, struggling with a mass of mis- cellanies in my pocket, "I've got her club money, some- where, and Meg's too. How much do you want?" "Half-a-crown from Pierre, one and three from Meg." "And I've got three and ten. Azubah here's your penny, and now lean look the whole world, including Kittums, in the face." "You've brass enough," said that young lady. "What were you and Ginger talking about on the stairs ? " "Mind your own business, Kit. turns." "You know," said Molly kindly, "if he was to dye his hair, he wouldn't be so very ill looking." "Who? Ginger? lam quite of your opinion, but if I might venture to interrupt your maiden meditations, I would remind you that those cashmere vests are marked urgent, and if they are left here till Monday morning, Miss North will know the reason why." "No peace for the wicked," sighed Molly, beginning to fold her work. But with my help, it was soon disposed of, and we hastened into the open air, with the exhilarating eon- sciousnes of a half day holiday before us. FREDA GREY ; 4. • 4.1 58i.:4eoci ,rs;

A company has been incorporated under the Com- panies Acts, 1862 to 1890, under the name of the Snow:, don Mountain Trarnroad and Hotel Company, the ouje9: of which is to construct and woik a tramroad about 4:I miles in length from Llanberis to a point at the surann: of Snowdon ; to acquire a lease of, and to carry on, well-known Victoria Hotel, Llanberis, situated near Of? commencement of the tramroad ;to erect, furnish, a nci carry on the Summit Hotel at the upper terminus of the tramroad, 3,500 feet above thP sea level. The capital will be £70,000, divided into 7,000 shares of £lO each: ~ The subscription list opened on Thursday of the presel,l! week, and will close on or before Wednesday May The Victoria Hotel has been in the Company's possession since November last, and many and extensive improve-_ ments have been made, and the tramroad is being pushet! forward rapidly, more than half of the line being forma._ and partly ballasted. The tram r -oad stars near to terminus of the L. & N.-W. railway at Llanberis, an"; there will be two intermediate stations, and the termioo station will be at the summit of Snowdon.The CamPaZ are also in possession of 32 acres of land adjoining Victoria Hotel, in which is situated the celebrated Pa 105.. darn castle together with the exclusive right of fish2og . in the upper lake. The Company has also Obtained f` et Mr. Assheton-Smith, a grant of certain rights in resPeL. of the water power above the waterfall of Commit Maw, at, which can be applied in making dynamos to 'gene! ere i i electricity for lighting and traction. The directors have voured to a rriue at a reasonable estimate of the proba do traffic receipts and working expenses of the tranircls. and also adding a fair sum they expect from the "—the., and they have come to the cone) asion that When - ' 0 undertaking is in full working order, the profits slir, not be less than eight per cent. upon the amount of 80,, capital. They have come to this conclusion by cowilp tug foreign mountain lines, there being no siruilaLt th • in the United Kingdom. The engineers expect tramroad will be reany for traffic during the e„"-nutiai season. The line will be similar to the Swiss rndient railways. The guage will be 2ft. 71in.. the gra, never steepen that one in 5i the nosteurves sharpe`,ltai 264 for the radius. The mode of going up the ra°lli tbe'• will be by cog wheels and the carriages will be anpll tram car type, each carriage seating 50 persouhs,loy two carriages forming one train. The journey elle;i1 riot will occupy less than one hour. The tramroad 171:et, in any way effect the natural beauts of the distr,l-for fact it will not be to the interest of the coMPs3l,,mber "'- to do so. It is expected to add greatly to the ,117.,„g1aS of tourists in this district. The engineer is Sir muLTier Fox and the contractors Messrs. Holme and XiDg' pool. - elected'

COUNTY OF CHESTER. -- DISEASES OF ANIMALS ACT, 1895. RABIES ORDER, 1895. -- MUZZLING ON' DOGS. -- NOTICE is Hereby Given, that at a Meeting of the Local Authority of the Coanty of Chester, under the above Act, held at Chester Castle, on Thursday, the 16th day of May, 1895, it was ordered that from and after the 22nd day of May instant, for an Area embrac- ing that portion of the County under the jurisdiction of the Local Authority of the said County, known as the BROXTON RUNCORN AND EDDISBURY WIRRAL POLICE DISTRICTS. the exemption from Muzzling, provided in certain Regulations made by the said Local Authority on the 2nd day of March, 1893, be revoked, the effect of which Order is that the Regulations made by the said Local Authority on the 9th day of December, 1892, and which provide for the MUZZLING OF ALL ; DOGS (with the I exception of Packs of Hounds, or Greyhounds, while being exercised or used fcr sporting purposes, or other Sporting:Dogs while being used for sporting purposes, or any Dogs while being used for the capture or destruc- tion of vermin, and in every case in charge of competent persons), are now in operation within the Area herein prescribed until further modified or revoked. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 16th May, 1895. --- NOTICE. In consequence of the foregoing revocation of exemp- tion, no Dog other than an exempted Dog or Dogs as mentioned in the Regulations made on the said 9th day of December, 1892, is allowed to be in or on any Public Place within the foregoing Area, unless such Dog is Muzzled with a Muzzle so constructed as to render it impossible for such Dog while wearing the same to bite any Person or Animal, but not so as to prevent such Dog from breathing freely or lapping water. Information as to the Townships comprised within the foregoing Police Districts can be obtained from any Police Constable of the Cheshire Constabulary.
